But that cannot help the imputation of Adam's actual sin to all men: for actions belong to individuals (supposits), not to genus or species; and when the proper differences by which they are distinguished among themselves are set down, all men are no more Adam than any other man whatever is: for Adam is contained under the species of man no less than the remaining individual men. Or do you mean that all men were considered as one man numerically in Adam? Nothing falser could be feigned than that consideration. What, then, do you mean by this proposition? I frankly confess I do not understand what sense not foolish it can have.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR 1 Augustine/Martyr; PLAC — divine act not answered
english: GAR. Response 1. That all men were one man in Adam is not a recent fiction, but the old doctrine of the Catholics, and namely of Augustine disputing against the Pelagians, which he often repeats in his works. Let one place from Epistle 106 to Boniface suffice for now: Whoever from that one were to be many in themselves were one man in him. If you ask Augustine whence he has it, he will answer that he has it from the Apostle, where he testifies that all sinned in Adam. They sinned in Adam: therefore they were one in Adam. Which Martyr also, one of the weightiest theologians whose authority the learned man urges in this matter, clearly signified when he wrote that Adam's sinning was the same as if all had been present and had sinned with Adam. PLAC. He answers something other than I asked. For I did not ask whence he had it that all men were one man in Adam, but whence he had it that God had considered all men as one man in Adam, so that He immediately imputed to them that first actual sin of Adam. The debate was about that consideration, about that inner act of the divine mind—on which, however, there is deep silence in this reply.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC proves conceded; GAR 2 in quo / PLAC deny immediate
english: Next I asked whence he had it—that is, from what divine Scripture. For such an act of the divine mind cannot be known from elsewhere than from God's revelation. But he flees to Augustine and Martyr, to whom such a divine act was not, I think, revealed from heaven by name. Then I did not deny that all men were somehow one in Adam—namely by unity of species and of origin; I only denied that it follows from that that they were so considered by God as one that He immediately imputed to them Adam's first actual sin. I also denied that they were considered as one numerically, or as an individual man. Therefore he proves what I concede; what I deny he does not even touch. GAR. 2. Since the Apostolic words 'in whom all sinned' denote the imputation of Adam's sin, as was confirmed above, and that imputation is an act of God declaring all guilty on account of Adam's sin, it follows that if those words signify that all were considered in Adam as one man, they designate by the same reason that they were so considered by God. PLAC. Neither did the Apostle say that all sinned in Adam; nor, if he had said it, would those words denote the imputation of Adam's sin, at least not immediate, as we both showed above and will confirm below.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR 3 origin+representation; PLAC origin ≠ representation
english: GAR. 3. All are said to have been one man in Adam not by specific or numeric unity, but by unity of origin—because all are of one blood, Acts 17:26, and every earthly man is by origin nothing but Adam, as Augustine speaks, Retractations Book 1, chapter 13—and by unity of representation: for by one Adam all were represented, because one Adam sustained the person of all, as theologians also teach with one consent, and as the most distinguished Amyraut does not deny in the Theses on the three covenants, Thesis 8. From that double unity the imputation of Adam's sin is gathered. PLAC. I acknowledge unity of origin—although it is one thing for all men to be one man, or to be considered as one man, and another for all men to have one origin, that is, stock or principle. The latter follows from unity of origin, not the former. But I desire unity of representation to be proved to me from Scripture, and likewise that which is brought forward in place of proof, that one Adam by sinning sustained the person of all men. For I long to know whence that very thing is had. It is posited by some, but proved by no one.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC — no Scripture for representation; forum tip before GAR 4
english: Did God then reveal it in Scripture? Let the place be produced. Can it be gathered from nature? Let a reason be adduced. For to one affirming something of that kind I am neither bound nor is it expedient to assent beyond the book of nature and of Scripture. Nor indeed can it be gathered from the words of Augustine or of the most distinguished Amyraut. For what consequence is this: every man is by origin nothing but Adam—therefore all men were considered by God as one man in Adam—or, therefore Adam in sinning sustained the person of all men? What the learned man says, that a natural conjunction can be a fit cause why someone should undergo penalties for another's crime, is not true in the divine forum, unless there is also between them a conjunction of sin, or at least in the one who is punished a sin worthy of that penalty, or he himself is a vessel of sins. What he subjoins, that because of unity of representation Adam's sinning was the same as if all had committed the sin, needs proof. For not whatever one who represents another does is at once to be imputed to that other, whether he consents or does not consent. God struck a covenant with the human race in Noah, and with the Israelites in Abraham; yet of neither, I think, were good works or sins imputed to their posterity.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR 4 — Rom. 5 / foedus; PLAC deny immediate
english: GAR. 4. The imputation of the first sin is gathered not simply from the fact that all are sprung from Adam, but from this: that we are so taught by the Apostle in Romans 5, as we have heard, and that by that sin Adam shook off all the grace of that primary covenant which had been struck in him with all men, as has often been said. PLAC. We are not taught by the Apostle in Rom. 5 the immediate imputation of the first sin. That neither the learned man nor anyone else has thus far proved, as may be seen partly from what has been said and partly from what is to be said. He adds another reason, but I do not understand it. For I would have him explain to me what covenant struck in Adam with all men he understands. For if he judges it to have been on this condition, that if Adam sinned his first actual sin would be immediately imputed to all his posterity, that covenant ought not to have been brought forward to prove immediate imputation. For it is no less in question than that imputation itself; and concerning it one may rightly ask whence it is had. From inspection of nature? Or from divine revelation through Scripture? For if it is had from elsewhere, for that very reason it ought to be rejected.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: body/republic metaphor; GAR Socrates/Crassus
english: Do you want all men to be considered as one republic, one body, whose head is Adam, and the remaining men each members? Then Adam was a head without a body, as we today are members without a head. GAR. This kind of reasoning, if it had come into L. Crassus's mind in that dissertation which he held with Q. Mucius Scaevola in Cicero, On the Orator, book 1, he could not by a plausible argument have turned aside Scaevola's saying that calls Socrates the fountain and head of the philosophers who in a long series flourished in Greece after Socrates was removed from human affairs—namely, because Socrates before those philosophers were born would have been a fountain without streams and a head without members; and those philosophers after Socrates would have been streams without a fountain and members without a head.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC Socrates fails; GAR physical vs moral head
english: PLAC. An excellent refutation! The discussion concerned Adam with reference to that time when he first sinned, long before he set himself to begetting us. I said that he was not yet then our head, as a general is head of an army, a magistrate of a republic, a king of a kingdom—because he would have been a head without members. Did Scaevola call Socrates fountain and head in that sense? With respect to that time, when there was not yet any hearer of his, nor any other philosopher besides him? Could or ought some action of Socrates therefore to be immediately imputed to all other philosophers? Nothing whatever descended from Socrates to the following philosophers by imputation. GAR. But if we treat the matter seriously, why should we not recall the most common distinction, so that head properly so called may be discerned from that improperly so called—that is, the physical from the moral? For in a physical head, which nature has bound by its nerves and ties with the rest of the body, the matter stands so that neither will it be called a head unless members are present, nor will members of the whole be so called unless they are actually joined with the head. But when theologians say Adam is the head of the human race, they without doubt use an improper signification, to denote that he is the origin and seminal principle of the human race, from which of course human nature took its beginning. Just as Abraham is called the head of the Jewish people.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC moral head; head-ratio ≠ immediate imputation
english: PLAC. Did the learned man think I had so lost my mind as to understand a head properly so called, when I said in express words an improperly so called, or moral, body, as a republic? For it is plain that a republic is not a physical body. And yet, although nature has not bound a republic to its kingly or magisterial head by nerves and ties, no one would say that a man was then head of the republic when he himself lived as a private person, the republic not yet born; nor will the republic which now is be called the body of that prince who a hundred or a thousand years ago ceased to be among the living. Such a head, such a political body, I understood. For otherwise I do not deny, nor have I ever denied, that Adam is the head of the human race in that sense which the learned man explains in this place. But what does that account of the head do for the immediate imputation of Adam's sin? Was Adam head in that way only while he sinned? Or because Abraham was head of the Jewish people, is some action of his in that way imputed to all and each of the Jews?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: reciprocity; peccavimus via propagation
english: And all Adam's sins ought to have been imputed to us, and all ours in turn to Adam; for the reason is equal: for what belongs to the head and what belongs to the other members suit the whole body. Those words also disturb me—'they are considered as one man in Adam'; for you seem to distinguish that one man from Adam. Further, whatever that consideration was, since it was outside us and put nothing either in Adam or in us, I cannot grasp in mind what it contributed to this—that we truly committed that actual sin of Adam so long before we existed. Add that if it endured while Adam was committing other sins, why are those also not equally imputed to us? But if it obtained only while he admitted that first one, I shall marvel either that we ceased to be in Adam immediately after that first sin was admitted, or that, although we were in him as before, we were nevertheless no longer considered as one man in him. You subjoin that we sinned in Adam. See how little difficult I am: I grant you that, provided you also grant me that we sinned in Adam in the same way in which we were in him. Now we were in him not because his being is imputed to us, or is a meritorious cause why we exist, but because by natural propagation through our intermediate parents he begot us. In the same way I confess that we sinned in him, because his sin by a long series of propagations begot our sin.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: infection/reatus; prefer corruption tip before Isaiah
english: For the rest, you shore up this answer of yours with questions. For, you say, who can otherwise give the reason of this infection and guilt? Why, I ask, did Adam by sinning destroy and subject to death not only a person but also the whole human nature—whereas other men by their actual sins wound persons and make themselves liable to death? How can an actual sin be justly imputed to us which we ourselves neither did, nor ordered, nor advised, nor approved by any consent of our will, and which with respect to us was in no way voluntary? Can you give the reason of these things? Would it not then be better firmly to believe the propagation of inherent corruption and of the guilt which follows it—Scripture teaching, experience bearing witness—and to leave to God the mode which you do not grasp, than beside and against Scripture to invent an imputation equally, or more, hard to grasp, and one that perverts and stains the justice of God?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: Subjungis — prefer ignorance; Isaiah 55
english: You subjoin that this compels us to confess that that first sin of Adam was considered in another way, and by God's just judgment imputed and ascribed to the whole human nature. I would rather confess my ignorance; nor would I be ashamed of this confession: for I judge him blind who does not feel that he is ignorant of far more than he knows. How many things there are in nature whose reasons why they happen so we cannot give? Better that, in my judgment, than bursting into God's secret mind and ascribing to Him without any revelation a consideration and judgment which perhaps neither was nor becomes Him. For you know that word of Isaiah 55: my thoughts are not as your thoughts. As the heavens are high above the earth, so high are my thoughts above your thoughts. And that: who has known the mind of the Lord?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR affected ignorance (Job); PLAC modestia
english: GAR. Here indeed I also first profess that I prefer to believe that this is not the affected ignorance of which those speak in Job chapter 21 verse 14—'Depart from us; we do not want the knowledge of your ways'—rather than to foster some sinister opinion of the learned man. PLAC. What handle, I ask, did I give by those words for fostering a sinister opinion of me, or what is there in this modest and religious ignorance of mine, by which I refuse to be wise beyond Scripture, like to the abominable impiety of those criminals in Job?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR Miror Rom. 5 / Deut 29:29; PLAC internal act
english: GAR. I only marvel by what reason he judges that those who seek the cause of original corruption, and of all the penalties lying upon posterity from birth itself, in the imputation—and so the participation—of the first sin are bursting into God's secret mind, when he is not unaware that older and more recent theologians both teach this and profess that they drew it from the Apostle's doctrine in Romans 5, as will afterward be proved by most frequent testimonies. To press all these with so grave an accusation, as if by rash daring bursting into God's secret mind and crossing those limits which God set for man in Deuteronomy 29:29—I do not know whether it is sufficiently agreeable to faithfulness. PLAC. First the debate was about that inward act of God by which God was said to have considered all men as one man in Adam. Did the older and more recent theologians say that? Can that be gathered from the Apostle's doctrine in Romans 5? Did the learned man bring most frequent testimonies to prove it? To ascribe to God a consideration—a certain inward act of mind and will—beyond Scripture, beyond reason: what is it to burst into God's secret mind, if this is not?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC — Lavater vs imputation-only; Reformed prejudice
english: The same, I confess, can be said of that immediate imputation in which the cause of original corruption is sought, if indeed it cannot be gathered from the sacred letters. For that too is an inward act of the divine mind and will. In vain he loads me with prejudices; in vain he stirs up the minds of theologians against me: for I do not accuse them, but brotherly warn them to beware this reef for themselves. For it is human to err, but to persist in error when warned is very shameful and dangerous. And I marvel that Reformed theologians use against their own brothers such prejudices as once, and in this time, have more than anything hindered the knowing of the truth. For not what this man or that taught is the rule of our faith, but only that which our one Teacher taught through His Apostles and Prophets. But that imputation neither Scripture, nor most of the older theologians, nor certain more recent ones of fair name taught: and some the learned man himself praises against himself. Let Ludovicus Lavater, the distinguished Zurich theologian, be an example (for to have brought one example will suffice in this place), whose these words from the Commentary on 2 Chronicles 25 he cites at Cap. XVIII, page 629: Let each pay the penalties of his own crimes. God is not bound by this law. For He justly punishes in all men the sin of the first parents, which by the vice of origin is each one's own. What can more oppose the doctrine of the learned man, who everywhere affirms that the sin of the first parents becomes ours only by imputation?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: root propagates vice not actual-as-ours
english: What if I ask of you the reason why that first— for it wholly escapes me. Although you seem of your own accord, unasked, to have wished to give a reason, for you add these words: because, namely, Adam was the first man, the origin and stock, or root, of all men. I acknowledge it; from this I understand that he could, together with human nature, propagate his vice into posterity: but I deny that therefore his actual sin was ours, or ought to have been imputed to us; I deny that from that the consideration and judgment which you ascribe to God can be made out. I do not see how that actual sin of Adam, that singular action, was more our action, our sin, than his person was our person. If you see that, show it to me, I beg, and explain: I will hold great gratitude to you.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR cum corruptione; PLAC vitium originis tip
english: GAR. To this first disobedience, then—not indeed taken precisely by itself, but together with the corruption which it effected in Adam—is imputed to us, as the learned man above acknowledged; it will indeed also be ours through that imputation. Why then should not Adam's person also be imputed to us, and be said also to have been our person? Let the learned man either grant this, or condemn and eliminate his way of arguing: and confess what the fact is—it was never heard that alien persons are imputed, but that the imputation of actions is a thing worn in everyone's mouth and speech, etc. PLAC. In what sense I said—and how little that hinders the cause I am pleading—that that first action of disobedience with the corruption which it bore is imputed to us, was set out above at pages 162–163. What he gathers from that, that that action is ours also through that imputation, I do not acknowledge. For the corruption is ours because it was propagated into us. But that action becomes ours not by imputation, but, as Lavater said, by the vice of origin: because of course the vice of origin or corruption is the communication of that disobedience, and a habitual consent to it; and so it is not ours because it is imputed to us; but on the contrary it is imputed to us because it is ours.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: Chamier — actiones sunt suppositorum
english: Certainly Chamier denied that that action of Adam is our action, book 1 On the corruption of man, chapter 8, § 9. I say, he says, that no sin one in number can be common to all men. For sin is either a quality or an action. A quality, as original sin. An action, as any actual sin whatever. But no quality, one and the same in number, can be communicated to several subjects: as the whiteness which is in snow cannot be the same in number in a swan, or in wool. But actions are of individuals (supposits). Therefore the same homicide perpetrated by Cain cannot be by Lamech. Therefore I deny that that sin of Adam is Original sin. For it cannot be common to all, whether by number, because it is an action: or by species, because it is an individual act. And again in the same chapter § 11. Every sin is either a quality or an action, as we have said, of him of whom it is called a sin. But this act of Adam is neither a quality of ours: for it does not even exist: and therefore it cannot be a quality: then action and quality differ widely: nor is it even our act: because the same act in number is not of various subjects. Therefore that act of Adam is not our sin: much less is it our original. This reason of his is the same as this of mine: if Adam's action is ours, his subject is ours: for actions are of subjects.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC — judicial justice; ours before immediate
english: For justice not only does not require, but does not even suffer, that by judicial imputation a sin should become the sin of him whose sin it would otherwise not have been. For the judge would make a sinner of one otherwise not a sinner—which conflicts with the judge's office as much as anything can. Therefore the learned man observes in vain that alien persons are not imputed, but actions. For I was not arguing thus: if Adam's action is imputed to us, his person also is imputed to us. But I was contending that no fit cause can be given why that action should be imputed to us immediately; and among the rest I was excluding this—that that action of Adam is ours, and therefore is justly imputed to us. It was understood, then, to be ours not through immediate imputation, but before it: in which way it cannot be said why it is more ours than Adam's person itself. Therefore it is not what I said that the learned man attacks, but something else.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: other Adam sins / Rom. 5 / Seth–Noah tip
english: Meanwhile I ask: while he was committing other sins (for you will scarcely deny that he committed them), was he not even then the first man, the origin, stock, or root of all men? That he was, you will doubtless grant: were those also, then, considered in the same way, and by God's just judgment imputed to all men? If you deny, you must confess that this reason of the consideration, judgment, and imputation of the first sin which you brought forward is not this—because Adam was the first man, and the origin and stock of all men. If you affirm, the Apostle in Romans 5 will refute you, inculcating the unity of the sin as much as the unity of the man. I would also gladly ask about Seth, about Noah, and other such stocks of the whole human race that remains, whether their sins also were in the same way both considered and imputed to posterity. If they were, the Apostle in Romans 5 ought to have said many men, not one, and we, before we are born, are most wretched, who have committed so many sins. If they were not, I ask the reason of the distinction: but I fear I may be longer in this place than is necessary.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR head-fasciculus; PLAC mediate only
english: GAR. But what the theologians teach—that Adam sinned as the head of men, and that that first disobedience of his is rightly imputed to posterity—he shakes with various engines of questions and erotemata, to which others also add some things, all of which we will here bind into one fascicle. PLAC. Neither do I strip Adam of the title of head of men, nor do I deny that that first disobedience of his is rightly imputed to posterity, if it is understood to be imputed by means of the corruption propagated from it into us. I only deny that Adam so sinned as the head of men that his first disobedience can or ought to be imputed to us immediately. Now these questions are all excerpted partly from my Theses, partly from this later Manuscript, except one. Therefore not all are of this place; yet it will not be useless to keep them safe in this place from the learned man's replies: since in them the debate is about the cause on account of which that sin is said to be immediately imputed—to the investigating of which this chapter is destined.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR erotemata 1–7 on head/imputation
english: GAR. 1. If he sinned as the head of the human race, why ought he not also to have been punished under that title? 2. Why is Adam's sin rather imputed to posterity than posterity's to Adam? 3. Since Adam after that sin did not at once cease to be head, why are Adam's following sins not equally imputed to posterity as the first? 4. Why is actual sin, which is a transient action, rather said to be imputed than habitual, which was a permanent vice? 5. If the first act of sinning was an act of nature, why not also the first act of begetting? Yet no one would say that we in Adam begot Cain or Seth. 6. If as Christ's righteousness is imputed to us, so also Adam's sin is ours by imputation, why is Christ called our righteousness, but Adam is not also called our sin? 7. When we are said to have sinned in Adam, is it proper or improper speech? It cannot be called proper unless we say that something simultaneously is and is not: for properly speaking, when Adam sinned, we would have been, we would not have been. If it is not proper, it must be reduced to the proper. But what does it properly signify that we were in Adam, except that we draw origin from Adam, or that Adam's being is the cause of our being?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR Pelagian parallel; PLAC deny immediate-catholic tip
english: GAR. VII. But we answer. I. Generally. If there ought to be room for such pinpoint interrogations, the doctrine of Original corruption can be no less speciously harassed by the followers of Pelagius or Socinus than this doctrine of imputation is vexed here. For it would be asked 1. Why Adam's moral corruption rather infected posterity than posterity's corruption stained Adam? 2. Why Adam's sin necessarily descended into posterity, and that of other fathers not so? 3. Why Adam's sin hurt Cain, and Cain's sin hurt Adam not at all? 4. Why the first sin rather corrupted us than Adam's following sins? 5. Why was Adam freed from that corruption ... and all infants ... not freed? 6. Why is Christ called our righteousness and sanctification, and Adam not called our sin and corruption? These and other things can be asked against the doctrine of inborn corruption, which if they do not hinder the learned man from having to acknowledge that corruption, neither ought those little questions to be an impediment to us from persevering in the ancient and Catholic faith of imputation. PLAC. Is the faith of immediate imputation thus ancient and catholic? That has neither been proved thus far, nor can it be proved.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC Ad 1–2 — generation; universal corruption
english: But he opposes those questions about original corruption to ours in vain: for they are not equal, nor have they any proving force at all. I answer the first: Why did Adam's moral corruption rather infect posterity than posterity's corruption stain Adam? Because moral corruption is propagated in no other way than by carnal generation: and posterity are begotten from Adam, but Adam is not begotten from them. To the second: Why did Adam's sin necessarily descend into posterity, and that of other fathers not so? Because Adam's sin was a change of the last end, and so brought a universal corruption into Adam's nature: but the unclean could not but beget the unclean, flesh not but flesh. Now the sins of other fathers could not be causes of this kind of corruption, since it was already produced in them, but effects by which it exercised and preserved itself. Therefore although we have drawn it most nearly from our nearest parents, yet it ought to be ascribed to Adam as its first author and spring.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC Ad 3–5 — Cain; first vs later; elect liberation
english: To the third: Why did Adam's sin hurt Cain, and Cain's sin hurt Adam not at all? Because Adam begot Cain, not Cain Adam. To the fourth: Why did the first sin rather corrupt us than Adam's following sins? Because that corrupted Adam's nature; those followed corruption already made as effects follow a cause. To the fifth: Why was Adam freed from that corruption which by his action he procured for himself, and all infants, who have done no evil, are not freed? He was freed from the guilt of that corruption by the grace of justification, and from the inherence of penalties by the grace of regeneration, because he believed and repented; and he believed because he was elect. The same happens to all other elect. But why this one rather than that was elect can be ascribed to no other cause than the freest will of God, who does what He will with His own. And he begot not according to grace, but according to nature, conceiving corrupt ones, just as one circumcised by art begets the uncircumcised.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC Ad 6 — Christ vs Adam; vitium inherent
english: To the sixth: Why is Christ called our righteousness and sanctification, and Adam not called our sin and corruption? Because we are justified by no other righteousness, sanctified by no other power, than Christ's. Therefore in Him all our righteousness and sanctification is to be sought. We cannot similarly say that we are damned by no sin but Adam's. For we are guilty of many others too, and to the universal corruption which we drew from Adam we too often add many habits, or particular determinations to certain objects; and that very sin of Adam is not ours by gift, or by imputation as Christ's righteousness is, but by reason of the vice propagated from it and inherent in us, which has power to condemn us not because it is Adam's, or flowed from Adam, but because by its nature it is a vice opposed to God's law. I have answered his little questions for Pelagius and Socinus: now let us see how he answers ours.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR free/voluntary imputation; PLAC needs Scripture
english: GAR. We have a sure reply ready: that the imputation of the first sin is a free and voluntary action of God, from God's fixed counsel and judgment, not depending on the order of nature alone. And that no one was God's counselor, bound to know those things and to answer concerning them which God refused to reveal in His word. That it is enough for us to know the thing itself—namely that all sinned in Adam, and his guilt came upon all unto condemnation, and so that first sin descends upon all by imputation. That the reasons of that judgment are with God, whose ways are unsearchable, and His judgments a great deep. Romans 11:33. Psalm 36:7. PLAC. If the immediate imputation of the first sin is a free and voluntary action of God, it cannot be known unless it has been revealed in Scripture. But it is not revealed in Scripture, nor do the places repeated here by the learned man have any force to prove it, as has partly already appeared, and will partly be made plain from what is to be said.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC free vs judicial; conscience tip
english: Next, if it is a free action of God, how is it a judicial action of God? For by free he means, I think, what can be omitted without any violation of justice or of law. How then is it called judicial, if neither law nor justice requires it of the Judge? If no one is bound to know those things which God refused to reveal in His word, certainly no one is bound to know that imputation—if, as I contend, God did not reveal it in His word. For the rest, by those questions I chiefly attack the reasons which are usually given why that one first sin is immediately imputed to us all. Therefore either those reasons must be renounced, and refuge taken in God's will alone, to whom it pleased to impute that one and not others, or our interrogations must be answered. Finally, since God does nothing except most wisely, and most justly, and most well, if such an imputation seems to clash with justice, or wisdom, or goodness, a pious conscience shrinks from ascribing it to God, and cannot force that upon itself unless either that clash is removed, or it is somehow compelled to believe it by express testimonies of Scripture—of which there are in fact none.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR erotema 1 foedus-head; PLAC knot tip
english: GAR. And yet the knots of the questions are not to be thought insoluble. Therefore now in the second place let us consider the erotemata one by one. It is asked first: If Adam sinned as the head of the race, why ought he not to be punished as head? Reply: When the name of head is given to Adam, account is taken not only of carnal origin, but also of that universal covenant which God struck in Adam with the human race. When therefore he is said to have sinned as head, it denotes not only that he was the radical principle of the whole race, but also that he was constituted head and principle of the race on this condition: that as soon as he turned aside from the obedience prescribed, not he alone would be bound by the guilt of his sin, but he would also make all posterity guilty, and so worthy of penalty. This, then, is what it is to have sinned as head: to have involved himself and posterity in guilt on account of that sin. PLAC. So the knot is not loosed, but enlarged by another knot: for besides that free and voluntary action which was ascribed to God without Scripture, see another—namely the pact of some universal covenant, of which there is not even a syllable in Scripture; and what is worse, a condition is invented hardly worthy of God.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC foedus-condition damnosum / hereditary corruption
english: For if He contracts any covenant with man, He does it for man's sake, and because it is good for man. But this covenant, whose condition is what the Learned Man declares, could not but be harmful to Adam's posterity. For far more evil was to be feared from it than good hoped for: since for any utility to return from it to us, Adam had to persevere through the whole course of life in obedience and faith toward God; and yet even then, if the Learned Man is believed, his obedience would not have been imputed to us—he would only have begotten us such as he was; but if he once turned aside from obedience, his first disobedience was to be imputed to us all unto the guilt of eternal death, and not that only, but that we might be punished for that imputed sin there was to be inflicted on us that hereditary corruption which is truly sin, and the fountain of sins. How came it that God, who is goodness itself and loved the human race, did not offer it a fairer condition, and that Adam did not ask God—seeing he was contracting with God as procurator of the whole human race—to obtain from Him a more tolerable condition? For surely such a condition might seem to have sprung from hatred rather than love; nor is it in any way understood how it could of itself contribute to God's glory, as all things God does ought.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC mandate vs threat; divine will beyond Scripture tip
english: Add that on that account the command would have belonged to Adam one way, the threat another: the former as to the head of the human race, the latter as to a private person; and conversely the threat would have belonged to us, not likewise the command. Finally, why was that covenant not contracted on this condition, that as he sinned, so also he should be punished as head of the human race? If you fall back on the will of God, what need was there of any other answer to these questions than that general one, because God so willed? But see that you do not ascribe to Him a will suited to your own ingenuity, least fitting to His virtues, and beyond Scripture.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR erotema 2 — why Adam to posterity, not reverse
english: GAR. It is asked second: Why is Adam's sin rather imputed to posterity than posterity's to Adam? Reply 1. This is because all posterity were in Adam radically and seminarily. Adam was not in posterity in this way. 2. That to impute sin is to inflict penalty on account of sin. But penalty always follows sin in the order of nature, never precedes it. Therefore Adam could not pay penalties for sins that did not yet exist, especially since not he, but Christ, ought to bear the sins of men, and by bearing to expiate them.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC vs head-body reciprocity; free imputation
english: PLAC. By this interrogation I did not immediately attack the immediate imputation of the first sin, but the reason by which it was fortified—namely that that first sin of Adam is imputed to all his posterity because Adam composed with his posterity one body of which he was head, we all his posterity members, and what the head does is imputed to the whole body: I objected that if this reason holds, there is no cause why what the members do should not likewise be imputed to the head, or even to the whole body, because the relation of head and members is reciprocal. And so, not attending to my mind, and to the circumstance of the place whence he drew this interrogation, the Learned Man does not answer to the point. For as to his first reply: first, it is not of the nature of a head that members be in it radically and seminarily. Next, if the question were of natural propagation, it would indeed be an excellent reason why sin was propagated from Adam into posterity rather than from posterity into Adam, because posterity are from Adam, not Adam from posterity; but when the matter is immediate imputation, which is a free act of God, if He regarded Adam's posterity as his members composing one body with him, why could God not equally impute posterity's sin to Adam and Adam's to posterity—especially since posterity were in no way the cause of Adam's sin, but Adam was the cause of posterity's sin?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC poena-order tip; GAR erotema 3 later sins
english: As for his other reply: first, while Adam lived his sons and grandsons sinned. Next, the judgment of the last day, and the penalty that will follow, will be later than the sins of Adam's posterity, and indeed of all of them. Third, since imputation is an act of God, and God then had present all Adam's posterity, He also had present their sins—why then could He not impute them? Finally, if penalty always follows sin in the order of nature and never precedes it, surely also sin in the order of nature always follows the existence of him to whom it is imputed, and never precedes it. GAR. It is asked third. Since Adam after that first sin did not at once cease to be head of the human race, why are his following sins not equally imputed as the first? Reply 1. Because the Apostle mentions one offense and disobedience of one man, not several, on account of which men were constituted sinners. 2. Because by that first sin of his Adam was shaken out of the benefit of that covenant which God had struck with the whole race in Adam's person. And so even if he did not cease to be head by relation of origin, he did cease by relation of covenant. For the imputation of which we speak, both were necessary: that Adam be both the root whence the human race should arise, and depositary of the covenant which he might keep or lose for himself and his. When therefore this later relation of head ceased through that first sin of disobedience, it is no wonder if Adam's following sins are not imputed, since in committing them he no longer sustained that former person, nor was head in the way God had at first constituted him.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC one offense / dual-foedus critique tip
english: PLAC. The Apostle mentions one offense and disobedience of one man because that one offense corrupted the nature of one man, and such nature as that one had, such he propagated into his posterity. But what is this to an antecedent imputation which the Apostle did not teach, and which is thought to precede all natural propagation and to hang on God's will alone? The reason remains: if that first disobedience is imputed because when Adam committed it he was our head, then when he committed others he was also our head, and his other disobediences ought to have been imputed to us—for the reason is the same on both sides. To the other reply, which he again fetches from I know not what covenant he had already mentioned several times, I say that covenant is neither taught in the sacred letters, nor becoming to God, nor was any benefit of it constituted against us rather than for us; and even if Adam had been shaken out of its benefit, if it was any, there would still have remained the binding force to obedience, and if it were less performed, to increasing the penalty. Otherwise what was that covenant? The same as the covenant they call of nature, or different from it? If the same, Adam remained bound to obey the law of the covenant of nature, and all his sins were violations of that covenant: why then did he not also remain head of the race by relation of that covenant? If different, then two covenants were contracted with Adam and the human race, one of nature, the other—how shall it be named (for it was certainly not of grace)—and why is violation of this rather imputed to the whole human race than of that which, being of nature, belongs to the whole nature of men? Add that I do not understand why that covenant constituted Adam head of men which long ceased to be before Adam begot anyone; nor how Adam is called head of the human race by relation to that covenant under which his posterity never were. Surely he was not head of posterity if, before any of his posterity existed, he ceased to be their head; nor, I think, is he called head by relation of covenant, but rather by relation to posterity founded in generation. So he would not have been head except at the moment he sinned—that is, he would not have been head except when they did not yet exist of whom he would be called head, and when they existed he would no longer have been their head: let him digest that who can; I certainly cannot digest it.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR erotema 4 — actual vs habitual; Apostolic tip
english: GAR. It is asked fourth. Why is Adam's actual sin imputed as of the head, which yet was a transient act; and why is the habitual not imputed, or Adam's corruption, which was a permanent vice? Reply 1. This is to be sought from the Apostle, who in this matter sets forth the fall and actual disobedience, but does not set forth the habit of corruption following from that disobedience. PLAC. Why should I seek it from the Apostle, who did not teach that imputation which I attack? Next, if the Apostle sets forth no habit of corruption following from that disobedience, Pighius cannot be refuted from the Apostle, nor can habitual corruption be proved.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC Pighius / GAR 2 actions not habits
english: How foreign that is from the doctrine of those by whose labors God reformed the Church, no one not quite a stranger in their books fails easily to see. GAR. 2. Since in the imputation of another's sin not habits but actions are imputed, as can appear to anyone who runs through all those examples produced above in great number, what wonder if also in this case not a habit but only Adam's act is remembered? PLAC. If habits are sins, if they make those in whom they are guilty, why can they not be imputed? Certainly, no less than our actual sins, they were imputed to our Surety, that He might satisfy for their guilt. And if any imputation of others' sins was made, whence do you have it that actual sins were imputed separated from habitual ones? And even if that could be proved, still there is a peculiar reason in the habit of Adam's corruption, which was a sin of nature, while its cause, actual disobedience, was rather a sin of the person; the former is propagated with nature, the latter not likewise.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR 3 commit-habit; PLAC omission / origin tip
english: GAR. 3. To impute another's sin to someone is to hold him in the same place as if in his own person he himself had perpetrated or committed the sin. But habits are neither perpetrated nor committed. Therefore they are not imputed. PLAC. What then will become of the sin of omission? For it is not properly perpetrated or committed: rather omission is opposed to commission. You see also, reader, that from this it follows that the habitual sin of origin, or corruption, is not truly sin: for every true sin is imputed, unless it is forgiven; and to forgive is not to impute sin.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR 4 foedus quamprimum; PLAC missing words tip
english: GAR. 4. On this account the covenant was conceived by God with Adam: that as soon as he violated it, he would bind himself and his with that guilt. But he violated it before he had put on the habit of corruption; and that actual sin was prior in nature to that habit. Therefore the act was imputed, not the habit. PLAC. Would that the learned man had reported the words in which that covenant was conceived! For if he did not know them, how could he know that it was conceived on that account? What is easier than thus to invent reasons?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC invented quamprimum; GAR effect/poena
english: But if the word 'as soon as' (quamprimum) was absent from those words in which it was conceived, why did the learned man insert and add it of his own? If in conceiving that covenant God used that word, whence does the learned man have it that it is to be taken in so precise a sense as to exclude the habit for this reason—that if not by some moment of time, perhaps by a moment of nature, actual sin was followed? GAR. If a comparison is instituted between Adam's actual disobedience and the ensuing habitual corruption, we shall see that this corruption was an effect of that disobedience, and so a penalty by God's just judgment of that actual sin. But penalty is not imputed; rather the sin which is the meritorious cause of that penalty. What wonder, then, if that disobedience was rather imputed than this corruption?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC corruption still sin / imputable tip
english: PLAC. Here again it is denied that corruption is imputed, that it is sin, and a doctrine so opposed to the confessions of Protestant faith is driven in. As for his saying that corruption is an effect of that actual disobedience: if he takes effect in a somewhat looser sense, it may be admitted. For it stands to that disobedience as heat to the heating by which it is produced. But what he deduces from that—that it is the penalty of that disobedience—does not necessarily follow: for not every effect of a sin is its penalty. Certainly habits are not properly either rewards of good acts or penalties of bad ones. How corruption is a penalty, and can be ascribed to God's just judgment, has been explained above and will be explained below as well. For the rest, in whatever sense it is called penalty, that does not hinder it from being a sin worthy of another penalty, and therefore imputable.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR erotema 5 — first generative act; Cain/Seth tip
english: GAR. Fifth it is asked. If the first act of sinning was an act of nature, why not also the first act of generating, so that in Adam we should be said to have been begotten as Cain, or as Seth? Reply. I pass over the learned man's paralogism, which ascribes Seth's begetting to the first act by which Adam generated, though that could only have been the third, Gen. 4. PLAC. What, I ask, is this paralogism? I fear it rather belongs to the Learned Man, who does not seem to have noticed the force of the disjunction I had used; namely there was a twofold act of Adam's generating: one absolutely first, the other first in the kind of those from whom we spring.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC duplex generative; GAR deficient-nature act
english: That was the act by which he begot Cain, this by which he begot Seth: for from Seth, not from Cain, we all draw our origin: I embraced both, lest any escape should lie open. GAR. To the matter itself I say: not every first act of nature was to be imputed to posterity (for Scripture neither openly testifies this, nor even lightly hints it) but only the first act of a nature failing from that perfection which God had given it in creation, and with the threat changed: in the day you first eat of the forbidden fruit, dying you shall die. Since therefore the first act of generating was in itself no act of a nature rebelling and failing from the Creator, any more than the first act of breathing, digesting, walking, &c.; but that first disobedience was the first act of a failing nature, whereby Adam most basely fell from the primary covenant—no one ought to wonder if both the first act of sinning is imputed to posterity, and the first act of generating is not.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC not any first act — why deficient over non-deficient
english: PLAC. Therefore that disobedience of Adam is not imputed to us insofar as it is an act of Adam: for many other acts of his are not imputed; nor insofar as it is his first act—for it was not absolutely first, but only first in its kind; nor insofar as it is in its kind the first act of nature—for that also fits other acts; but insofar as it is an act of a failing nature. Now this is asked: why ought an act of a failing nature rather be imputed to us than an act of a nature not failing? For that, as I see, is from the failing of nature, not from nature itself. For what reason, when the rest are equal, should evil rather be imputed to us than good?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC being before sinning; generative presupposed
english: For if sinning follows being, as it certainly ought (for of what is not there are no accidents), the act of generating is that by whose force we first are; this ought to seem to follow, and in it to be founded that act by whose force we first are sinners; at least this does not make us sinners except by means of that: and so it presupposes it: for to sin presupposes to be, and prior in the order of nature is that we become than that we become sinners. If therefore we were sinners by imputation of another's sin which becomes ours, that imputation ought to follow something by which we were humans, seeing that in nature's order we are humans before we are sinners, and the subject is prior to its accident.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC Seth-act precedes imputation tip
english: But that act by which we were first made humans is that act of generating by which Adam begot Seth: therefore the antecedent or immediate imputation of the first sin presupposes that act. Earlier, then, was it that we be counted as begotten from Adam than as sinners, and that first act by which we were begotten belonged to us earlier than that by which we were made sinners. For Adam's sin is imputed to us because we are his posterity; and we are his posterity because he begot us; and he begot us insofar as he begot Seth. Therefore the act by which he begot Seth precedes the imputation of sin in the order of nature. And yet, if the learned man is believed, Adam's sin was imputed to us long before he had begotten Seth, at the very time it was committed: either then it also preceded Adam's coming to be.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR erotema 6 Christ-righteousness parallel tip
english: GAR. Sixth it is asked. If as Christ's righteousness is imputed to us, so also Adam's sin is ours by imputation, why is Adam not called our sin as Christ is called our righteousness? Reply 1. That God speaks as He wills; that it is ours to be content with those phrases which occur in the Scriptures, and which set forth God's mind, so far as our salvation is concerned, clearly enough. Although therefore Scripture does not say Adam is our sin, yet it uses those locutions which manifestly mark imputation, of which enough was said before. PLAC. I do not remember using this reason or interrogation, nor do I know whose it is: yet whether mine or another's, it seems fitted to refute the major of the argument on which immediate imputation usually most leans—As we are constituted righteous through Christ, in the same way we were constituted sinners through Adam: for it shows a memorable difference between Christ and Adam.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC Christ/Adam phrase-disparity; no immediate locutions
english: But the word 'is said' in this interrogation is not to be taken relative to Scripture alone, as the learned man does, but relative to Scripture and all the theologians, who never said Adam is our sin, or our unrighteousness, or that we are unrighteousness in Adam. For the diversity of phrases when Christ and Adam are treated in the matter of justification and condemnation argues diversity and disparity between the two. And so it becomes us to be content with those phrases which occur in Scripture—and truly we are greatly content with them—yet it also becomes us to consider those phrases attentively, and to weigh the reasons why God thus or thus expressed His mind, or did not express it; in which the Apostles went before us by their example, sometimes even urging Scripture's very silence. But there are no locutions in the Apostle which manifestly mark immediate imputation; indeed none have been seen that mark it even obscurely.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR 2 Rom 5 comparison; PLAC abstains where compared
english: GAR. 2. In those places where Christ is called our righteousness, no comparison is instituted between Adam and Christ: which if it had been instituted, as was done in Romans 5, who does not know whether Paul would have used that phrase by which he would teach that Adam is our sin, as Christ is our righteousness, even if not altogether on the same account. PLAC. But I argue from this: that where the Apostle institutes no comparison between Christ and Adam he uses that locution of Christ, but where he institutes some comparison between the two he abstains from it. Although, as I said, respect is had not to Scripture alone but also to all the theologians, who never use that locution of Adam.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR 3 why not Adam our sin — external merit tip
english: GAR. 3. Yet a probable reason can be given why Adam is not called our sin as Christ is named our righteousness. For Christ is so called that it may be signified there is nothing internal and inherent in us by whose force and virtue we can stand before God's tribunal, or obtain absolution and remission of sins: and so all that is meritorious of our justification is outside us—namely the righteousness which is Christ's own, ours only by imputation. But no such thing can be said of Adam. For besides that Adam's actual sin is meritorious of the penalties that lie on us, there is also something internal and inherent in us by whose desert we also lie under condemnation—namely our native corruption, which together with Adam's imputed sin makes as it were one body of guilt by which God in His judgment holds us liable. See then a cause why Scripture did not say Adam is our sin as it said Christ is our righteousness.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC mode-difference; gift vs imputation clash
english: PLAC. The learned man therefore acknowledges that we are not constituted sinners before God's tribunal by Adam's disobedience in altogether the same mode in which we are constituted righteous by Christ's obedience: and so that likeness is not to be pressed as if there were no difference in the mode: and this is the whole of what we meant to prove by this interrogation, if indeed we used it. Therefore his reply fights for us, not against us. Yet some things in it seem worthy of censure. First, that he says Christ's righteousness is ours only by imputation: for if likewise, as he everywhere contends, Adam's sin is ours only by imputation, both are ours in the same mode, and there is no difference in that point. That clashes with the Apostle, who hints a very great difference in the mode by which Christ's righteousness and Adam's unrighteousness are ours, when he calls the former a gift, and grace, and a donation which is of grace: for so he signifies the mode by which it becomes ours—a mode in which Adam's sin neither was made ours, nor could be.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC inherent corruption vs immediate extra us tip
english: Next, to what end does he observe here that Christ's own righteousness is ours only by imputation, if he holds the same of the sin that is Adam's own—that it likewise is ours only by imputation? What does that do to explain the difference between Christ and Adam? Or if he does not hold that, he contradicts himself, seeing he has driven it home several times. Further, if there is something internal and inherent in us by whose desert we lie under condemnation, why, not content with that desert and that condemnation, do we want another sin placed outside us to be immediately imputed? You will say: that it may be the cause of this internal thing, which otherwise we would lack. God then delights in this internal sin, seeing that without any necessity He freely imputes to us that sin placed outside us, so that by the force of that imputation that internal sin may be produced in us which otherwise could not be produced. Is this to glorify God, and not rather to make Him (which I cannot pronounce without horror of conscience) the author of our sin?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC corpus reatus / infants death — Confessio tip
english: Finally, how do that imputed sin and native corruption make as it were one body of guilt, if the latter is properly the penalty of the former? For guilt precedes penalty; and the imputed sin that so makes us guilty that we are worthy of that corruption and eternal death—its guilt does not seem a halved guilt, but perfect and whole. And if they compose one body of guilt, either the Apostle in Romans 5 understood that whole guilt—and so we are condemned through Adam in another mode than we are justified through Christ, which the learned man everywhere denies—or he understood only half that guilt's part, which I think no one has said. The last question it seemed good to defer to its own place, which will soon occur. You go on asking: What reason, you say, can be assigned why little ones who have not yet sinned actually should die, whether in their mothers' womb, or in being born, or right after birth, unless this—that Adam's sin, through which death pervaded all men, is imputed to them? I ask on the contrary: what reason can be assigned why Adam's actual sin, committed so long before they began to be, should be imputed unto death to little ones who have not yet attained the use of reason? Meanwhile I satisfy your question: I assign the reason—the vice inherent in them from conception. I call as witness the Confession of Faith, Article XI.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: Confessio XI inherent vice; GAR unsatisfied tip
english: We believe this vice is truly sin, which makes all and each of men—little ones not excepted, even while still hiding in their mothers' womb—guilty of eternal death before God. You had seen this reason: why did you not rest in it? It does not satisfy, you say, if someone says they are sinners because stained with sin, and so mortal. That is indeed true, but it must necessarily be admitted that they have no sin except that original, which is not their own sin except insofar as they are sons of Adam; and insofar as sprung and begotten from him, they sinned in him, and his disobedience and guilt is imputed to them. Either I do not understand you, or here you begin to open what you think: that there is no original sin besides that actual sin of Adam imputed to us.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC vs Pighius — hereditary vice proximate death-cause
english: Which was the opinion of Pighius and Catharinus and Salmeron, rightly condemned by our Churches: for if you believe there is in infants an original inherent vice which is truly sin, which suffices for damning the human race, which makes infants hiding in the maternal womb guilty of eternal death before God—why, when you ask why infants die, does it not satisfy the one who answers that in them the cause of death is the vice or sin hereditarily inherent? For this is to give the proximate cause of infants' death, whose remote cause is Adam's fall.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: Job/Christ unclean begets unclean; soul-transfer deferral
english: If again you ask why this vice is in little children, I will answer with Job, that from the unclean a clean cannot be made, and with Christ Himself, that what is born of flesh is flesh. As man begot man, so the unclean begot the unclean, the corrupt the corrupt, according to nature's laws. Why then does this answer not satisfy you? Is it because you do not grasp how vice can be propagated and poured from parent into the offspring's soul? Yet there is no difficulty in that matter beyond what arises from the creation of the rational soul—which difficulty I tried to remove in my theses by a reason which you, because you did not understand it, carp at in the last chapter of your treatise, but in no way refute. For it is vain labor to refute what is not understood. When I come to that place, God helping, I will explain myself. Or is it because you do not grasp how one actual sin could bring into Adam a moral corruption to be propagated with the nature? Yet I had given the reason of this in the theses, which I have not read rejected or blamed by you in this whole treatise of yours.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC fountain of evils in race not God; last-end change
english: Shall I say frankly what differs between your opinion and mine? I aim that the fountain and cause of all the human race's evils be referred to the human race itself, not to God. But your opinion looks to attributing it to God Himself: which I, by the reverence I bear toward my Creator and Redeemer, cannot endure. Inherent vice is the fountain of all actual sins. It is agreed between us that it draws origin from Adam's first actual sin. But it is asked first: what is the reason why that first actual sin corrupted Adam? I ascribe it to the very nature of that first sin, which was a change of the highest good, or last end—that is, apostasy from God as envious and malevolent, and turning to creatures as to the highest good or last end, against God's word. And since whatever we desire is either an end or a means to an end, and the last end contains bound to itself all means and all subordinate ends, when it was changed there followed a universal change of all that was moral in Adam; which change a bad conscience fleeing and dreading God—as offended, as angry, as judge, as enemy—increased and confirmed. But you do not hesitate to ascribe whatever it is to God Himself, who withdrew righteousness from Adam and deprived him of uprightness and holiness, so as thus to punish the actual sin and satisfy His justice.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: Why corrupted Adam begets corrupted — nature infects
english: It is asked second: why did Adam, corrupted and vitiated by sin, beget sons similarly corrupted? I attribute that to the nature of that corruption which, being universal, corrupted and infected the generative force itself, insofar as it is a certain moral faculty, and turned it to generation not as to a means but as to a last end. Further, the last end, since it is not defined or dependent on another but all things on it, is infinite by its nature. And so the faculties are carried toward it without limitation or measure, in a way infinitely. After therefore in place of the true last end, that is God, there succeeded a falsely appearing, deceitful appearance of happiness to be found in creatures, the generative faculty dealt with generation immoderately, without bridle, without limitation, corruptly and depravedly, as around a last end—the superior part of the soul turned the same way together with the sensitive appetite, not restraining but driving.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: Generative faculty corrupted as moral tip
english: From a faculty so corrupted and acting depravedly a corrupt seed was wrought—that is, agreeable and congruent with the depraved generative faculty, and also with the other faculties which the generative power tries as accurately as possible to sketch and express in the seed. But how this viciousness passes from seed to the rational soul I will explain, God granting, in its place—that is, at the last chapter of your treatise. GAR. First we ask of him what he elsewhere asked of us: Whence do you have that? From the Scriptures, or from elsewhere? Or how do you show this is not to be counted among fictions which delight the curious with an empty shade of subtlety? PLAC. I asked whence you had it, when I was disputing, of what he said about a certain internal act of the divine mind and will, to be known from nowhere but divine revelation. But here what have I said of that sort which cannot be firmed by Scripture, or by reason, or by experience itself?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR — generative faculty not moral; Decalogue tip
english: GAR. But I scarcely trusted my eyes when I read that the generative faculty could have a place among the moral faculties: Will moral philosophy also snatch it hereafter from the physicists and physicians as from possessors of bad faith, and claim it as her own peculiar? What has that faculty, that it ought rather to be raised to the dignity of morals than the concoctive, or nutritive, or augmentative, which philosophers have hitherto taught are not partakers of reason, but by their nature brute and unaware of themselves, and which belong to man not as he is man, but as he has a nature common with other animals? Finally, what law of the Decalogue is there to whose precept the faculty of generating is to be believed subject? For all, I hope, agree that morals are bounded by the Decalogue. But at least it is subject to morals. Nay, not even that is simply true; otherwise it would always be moved by the empire of the will, which it is certain often happens otherwise. Nor does a woman always either conceive when she wills, or not conceive when she does not will.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC three respects — generic, animal, human moral
english: PLAC. Did I simply say the generative faculty is a moral faculty? I only said: that the corruption of nature, being universal, corrupted even the generative faculty itself, insofar as it is a certain moral faculty. I therefore meant not that it is absolutely moral, but in a certain respect. And it can be viewed in three ways: first, as a certain faculty or generic property: so viewed it is a faculty of the vegetative soul, merely physical and brute, and aims to beget nothing but a vegetal thing. Second, as an animal faculty attempting the generation of an animal, and so the production of the sensitive soul itself: so it can be called a faculty of the sensitive soul, by whose sensitive appetite it is excited and applied to generating. Finally it can be viewed as a faculty of man depending somehow not only on the sensitive appetite but also on the will, and aiming at the generation not of a dog or lion or other brute animal, but of a man. So far it can be called moral, insofar as it works seed that a rational animal endowed with moral faculties may be produced, and is excited and applied to that by the moral faculties—will and sensitive appetite.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC Aristotle / Decalogue non concupisces tip
english: Just as therefore the sensitive appetite, though in its genus only sensitive, yet in man can be viewed insofar as it is somehow rational and, as Aristotle says, partaking of reason, and so is capable of virtue and can be ruled by law; so the generative faculty, though generically viewed in no way moral, yet insofar as it is a faculty of man, by whose appetite it is somehow ruled and which attempts generation—why can it not so far be called somehow moral? Which the learned man himself seems to hint enough when he says it is often not moved by the empire of the will: for he seems to concede that it is sometimes moved by the empire of the will. Why then can it not so far be called moral? I meant nothing else than that insofar as it depends on appetite or lust, and works seed suited to the moral faculties, it was so far corrupted, and as by nature's reason it tends to producing a man, so by reason of corruption it tends to producing a corrupt man. What in that is worthy of so sharp a rebuke? Indeed for the generative faculty, if viewed by that generic account of it, there is the same reason as for the nutritive or augmentative; but not if viewed by the specific account it has in man, on whose appetite it depends. For the concoctive as concoctive, or nutritive as nutritive, in no way depends on the will, but only accidentally, insofar as each follows the taking of food which depends on the will. But generation as such is somehow in the power of will or appetite: for fathers never generate without appetite concurring, and they can even abstain from generating perpetually if they will. Why then can the faculty of generating, like that of eating, not be ruled by law? And to what does the Decalogue's command, You shall not covet, pertain?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR many last ends if corruption turns all faculties
english: GAR. But these things set aside, what is this—that Adam's corruption turned the generative faculty to generation as to a last end? For that corruption, being universal, infected the other faculties no less than this one. Why then should it not be said to have turned the other faculties to their acts—the concoctive to concoction, the nutritive to nutrition, &c.—as to a last end? so that for the number of faculties there would also be a number of last ends. Which of those who know that man's last end can be only one would bear that?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC generative alone for propagation; false ends many
english: PLAC. And that corruption is universal, and infected the other faculties too, but for the purpose only the generative one mattered, because the matter was the propagation of man, through which that corruption is propagated. But neither, as I already noted, are concoction and nutrition, like the act of generating, infected with lust, and the generative faculty tries to propagate the other faculties as they are. Meanwhile it is certain the concoctive and nutritive do not perform their functions as perfectly after sin was committed as before: and so all men from infancy are liable to various diseases and death; yet concoction and nutrition are not last ends, but only subordinate to the conservation of the individual and the propagation of the species. The true last end can be only one, namely God. But a false last end is one only in genus, and multiple in species and number; for either pleasure is sought, or utility, or honor, and of these also, for the various things in which they are sought, there is a great variety.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR physical faculty vs user; PLAC only mind tip
english: GAR. Further, since a last end has relation to intermediate and subaltern ends, properly that will be a last end for those who can know the distinction of subaltern ends and the last: which, since it can fit neither that universal corruption nor the generative faculty or any other simply physical one, how will the generative faculty be said to be turned by corruption to generation as to a last end? Distinguishing rather between the faculty and the man who uses the faculty would have been better. For he can indeed by his understanding and will set himself a last end: but the physical faculty itself has the end to which it was determined by the Author of nature, which it always regards, whatever the corrupt man attempts—as the concoctive concoction, the generative generation, &c. PLAC. If the learned man reasons well, only the mind acts for an end, not the will: for the will does not properly know, much less know the distinction between the last end and the subordinate ones.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC only-mind reductio; lust pleasure; corrupt begets corrupt
english: Phantasy too and the sensitive appetite do not know that distinction. But if for a faculty to act for a last end it must know the distinction of the last end from the subordinate ones, then the faculty that tends to a subordinate last end must also have that same distinction known: and so, as I said, no faculty of man except the mind alone will act for an end. The same of universal nature, which the Philosophers are accustomed to prove acts for an end. Nothing therefore is falser than that proposition of the learned man. Further, when a man by mind and will tends to the true last end, all that is his tends the same way and is referred from it; but when he wanders from the true last end, all his faculties wander from that same end. Who does not know how prone lust is to abuse the generative faculty for pleasure? And when that faculty was given by God and destined to the procreation of a like, once universal corruption is set in the begetter, it cannot but be—not by God's fault but by the vice of the corrupt begetter—that it begets the corrupt, just as the generative faculty of a leper begets a leper: for it is determined to that thing not by the author of nature, but by the depravation of him whose faculty it is.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR — why generation not science/pleasure/externals?
english: GAR. Next, when the learned man proposes a last end which has succeeded into the place of the true end, falsely apparent—namely a fallacious species of happiness to be found in creatures—how does he at once leap to generation, that is, from a general end to a singular one? For he who acknowledges that another falsely apparent end has succeeded into the place of the true last end is not therefore at once compelled to conclude that that end must be generation. Why rather than science, or pleasure, or external goods, &c., unless a reason appear from elsewhere why generation rather than any other whatever should be said to have succeeded into the place of the true last end?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC coitus-pleasure = generation; carnal desire false happiness
english: PLAC. The learned man seems to me to play with these words and what follows, rather than to argue in earnest. For is not that fallacious species of happiness sought in many things? But why did I not rather say pleasure than generation? Namely because by the pleasure of coitus it seemed honest to signify that which I marvel either that the learned man did not notice, or, if he noticed, that he dissembled. For what, I ask, is the aim of carnal concupiscence and lust? the glory of God? the edification of the neighbor? Certainly it follows nothing but a fallacious shade of happiness and pleasure—which is plain in those who loosen the reins to such concupiscences: for they seek nothing else than to obtain what they desire and to satisfy lust. And so what the learned man adds does not seem to me to need any reply.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR even granting — still need imputation for posterity
english: GAR. But grant that all stand no otherwise than as it pleased the learned man: that the generative power is a moral faculty; that Adam's corruption turned it to generation as a last end; that the whole superior part of the soul with the sensitive appetite—that is, the whole Adam—was turned the same way; that corrupt seed flowed from these. Still all this would not have brought it about that that first corruption should stain those born of Adam, unless something else be added. For the same can happen in others. A man will contaminate himself with perjuries, adulteries, murders, &c., and will contract the worst habits from them; he will turn his generative power, sensitive appetite, and superior part of soul, and himself entire as much as he is, to generation as a last end: yet beyond those things by which he has drawn just condemnation on his own head, he will not by natural propagation derive it into posterity as was done in Adam. Something else therefore must have intervened in that first sin which does not so hold in other sins of fathers. Namely God, who has absolute right over his creatures, willed by most just judgment that that first sin of Adam be imputed to all his posterity: he does not so will other sins to descend upon all posterity.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC moral generative / lust / universal vs particular sins
english: PLAC. In what sense the generative faculty is called by me somehow moral, I have already set out—namely by reason of concupiscence or lust, and of destination to procreating a moral subject. It is also plain in what sense I said it was turned to the act of generating as to a last end—namely because lust looks at nothing but pleasure. So far also it is called by me corrupted, insofar as it tends not only to the propagation of man's faculties, but also to propagating corruption, in which it recedes from the purpose for which it was created. That uncleanness being set, it necessarily follows that those born of Adam are stained. But why does the same not happen in other sins? Because other sins did not bring universal corruption into the parents, but proceeded from it, and added nothing except certain particular determinations of that universal corruption toward seeking happiness rather in this thing than in that, in such a pleasure than in some other: and so it ought not to seem strange if universal corruption is propagated, while particular determinations or habits are not.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC false last-end propensity; regen; absolute-right tip
english: For that universal corruption is, in our judgment, set in a propensity to a false last end and an aversion from the true end. For the appetite of a last end is necessary, because it is appetited first of all. And so man had to be created with an appetite of the true end, and now must be born with an appetite of a falsely apparent end, if not in act at least in propensity, because of the change of last end induced into our nature by Adam's fall: which change is not made by perjuries, adulteries, and murders, and so those are not propagated. Hence such particular habits or determinations can somehow be corrected and changed, and not rarely we are bent from one vice to the opposite: but that universal corruption cannot be taken from us except by the grace of regeneration. But if this our reply does not please, I would rather at least say that the cause of this discrimination is that God was unwilling to hinder that first sin of Adam from being propagated, but was willing to hinder his other sins and those of other fathers from being propagated also. For this seems better than to invent an antecedent imputation—which nevertheless does not prevent that whole discrimination from being referred to God's will. For the rest, two things not well coherent seem here to be joined, when that imputation of Adam's sin is said to be done by God by his absolute right over creatures, and yet by most just judgment.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC absolute right vs most just judgment incoherence
