Let us now drop the rhetorics, and what is said of a penalty that is itself in kind the evil of fault—something was said of this above, and occasion will return later to dispute it more fully. Let us attend only to the force of the argument, which can be woven thus. That the just be involved with the unjust in the same condemnation and death is alien to God's justice, Abraham witnessing. But in the imputation of another's sin, the just would be involved with the unjust in the same condemnation and death. Therefore the imputation of another's sin is alien to God's justice. PLAC. On what occasion, and how aptly, Abraham's testimony was brought by me the prudent Reader will consider if he please. Meanwhile the Argument the learned man has woven here I gladly take as my own, provided that in the minor "imputation of another's sin" is not understood of any whatever, but only of that about which the dispute between us is—namely that which precedes every sin inhering in us or committed by us.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: GAR — all polluted; PLAC — first discrimen for mediate
english: GAR. Here it could first be answered that the cause Abraham debates is far from the Question of Adam's imputed disobedience. For Abraham speaks of those who were not all in the same condition, but some were just, others enslaved to injustice: and whose ratio was such that not only could the just be drawn into partnership of the same penalties for the impious with whom they were mixed, but also the impious could share the same benefit and preservation for the just; Whence Abraham pressed God with prayers for both—that the just not perish for the impious' crimes, and that the impious be pardoned for the just. Yet our business stands far otherwise. For first among those to whom Adam's sin is imputed, in this respect there is no distinction of justice or injustice; for not Adam alone is unjust and posterity just and innocent, but all are polluted by corruption of the seed's nature, as was explained in cap. 2. Next there are neither fifty nor twenty nor ten nor even one in this order of those carnally generated for whose justice God would or ought to spare the rest. So from Abraham's words no legitimate consequence against imputation of Adam's sin can be drawn. PLAC. Of these two discriminations the former is indeed apt if mediate imputation is in view, which presupposes and follows inhering corruption or injustice.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: PLAC — immediate makes injustice follow; tip before Ezek 21
english: For that is why we are involved in the same condemnation and death with unjust Adam—because we ourselves are unjust in ourselves: but if immediate imputation, which alone I impugn, is in view, that is false; for the imputation precedes hereditary corruption as the penalty of the fault. So our injustice follows this kind of imputation and condemnation as effect, and does not precede as cause. We are not involved in the same condemnation with unjust Adam because we are unjust, but on the contrary we are unjust because we are involved in the same condemnation with unjust Adam: for so by imputation of the actual sin Adam committed we are made sinners—that is, guilty—and that that imputed sin may be punished we are made inherently unjust. Set aside this imputation or condemnation and Adam is the guilty one, we innocents. Therefore that imputation or condemnation, Abraham judging, clashes with God's justice. What the latter discrimination does for the matter at hand, I do not see.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: GAR — not simply concede; Ezek 21 sword cuts just and wicked
english: GAR. But against that solution one must go further in considering this Abrahamic deprecation. We say, then, that it is not to be conceded simply and absolutely that it wholly abhors God's justice that the just, or personally innocent, should sometimes be involved in the same penalty with the unjust and criminal, however much Abraham takes from that the argument of his plea. 1. because God himself testifies in express and clear words that he sometimes does the contrary. For so he addresses his prophet, Ezek. 21:8–9: Say to the land of Israel, Thus says Jehovah; behold, I will draw my sword from its sheath, that I may cut off from you the just and the wicked: that I may cut off from you the just and the wicked: therefore my sword shall go forth from its sheath against all flesh from the South to the North.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: GAR flood/Sodom/Abimelech; PLAC — cuts not solves; what is justus?
english: 2. Because Abraham could not have been ignorant of certain examples of that divine dispensation which God had set before the eyes of all—first in the general flood, then in the overthrow of Sodom, third in Abimelech's household—all of which we produced above in their place. PLAC. But this is not to untie the knot, but to cut it. What if in Ezek. 21 by 'the just' is meant one who seems just to himself or to others, as it pleases some interpreters? What if 'just' is understood by comparison with others more wicked?—according to that word of Mic. 7:4: the best of them is like a thorn; the most upright is worse than a thorn-hedge.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: PLAC — justus readings; Noah/Lot spared; Abimelech after Gen 18
english: What of this—that there is no one at all who is just and who does not sin: all have sinned and are destitute of the glory of God: even infants newly born are polluted by inherent vice, and therefore worthy of those penalties with which they are afflicted by God's justice. I pass over that common penalties stand otherwise in the pious, otherwise in the impious. For in respect of the former they are chastisements and paternal penalties, and a commuting of a life liable to sin and misery into one perfectly holy and blessed; so no injury is done them—nor to the children of the impious, who so die for original sin, by which they are like their parents, that they are yet preserved from many sins they would have committed if life had been prolonged to them, and from many calamities into which they would have fallen; which can be counted for some benefit. Least of all, then, does this oracle of God in Ezekiel clash with Abraham's testimony. The examples of divine dispensation which the learned man subjoins stand against his cause. For God's justice did not involve Noah in the same condemnation with the impious in the general flood, nor Lot in the overthrow of Sodom. For the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation, but to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished: although the overthrow of Sodom followed and did not precede—as the learned man's slip of memory seems to suppose—that colloquy of Abraham with God. The same must be said of the example published in Abimelech's household: for its history is narrated only at Gen. 20, and is so narrated that Abimelech appears to have felt the same as Abraham concerning God's justice.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: GAR Pererius orator; PLAC — rejects Jesuit insult of Abraham
english: GAR. How then, you will say, does Abraham once and again in chapter 18 press that it ought to be far from God to destroy the just with the unjust? Reply 1. Some so treat this deprecation of Abraham that they not only deny the opinion he proves is altogether certain, but even affirm it has a manifold confutation. So Pererius, who when he sets out that confutation concludes at last in these words: Abraham, like an orator defending a worst cause, turning himself every way so that from wherever he can he may snatch any shield of defense, mixes words and varies sentences, wraps in reasons not very probable nor much fitting his purpose, and finally moves every stone to obtain what he asks of God, dealing with God not so much by the weight of sentences or the strength of arguments as by the heat of charity and the most burning affection of piety toward those wretched men. PLAC. Does the learned man approve, or disapprove, those words of Pererius? If he disapproves, why does he praise them? If he approves, I marvel that he could approve words so bold, and so injurious to so great a Patriarch, the father of believers, from a Jesuit. For my part, who by God's greatest gift believe myself a son of Abraham and rejoice in it, I can scarcely bear one speaking so shamelessly of my father. For how great was the Patriarch, confederate of God, friend of God, so often honored with God's colloquy, a distinguished Prophet? Who would believe he meant to defend a worst cause before God, and to use less probable reasons as if they were necessary? What of this—that God did not rebuke that reason but admitted it, and it becomes us believers to imitate the faith of the Father of believers?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: GAR Abraham's scruple; PLAC — strong assertions, judicial plea
english: GAR. 2. To Abraham this rule was indeed certain and unmoved, which no believer fails to acknowledge—that it can never at all come to pass that God should appoint anything unjust: but in the special case he could not see how this slaughter of innocents could agree with God's justice. He asks, therefore, not with a mind to resist, but that he may clear this scruple for himself, whether God is about to destroy the just with the wicked. So. PLAC. Are those then the words of one doubting, or simply asking: Far be it from you to do any such thing, delivering the just to death with the unjust, so that it should be with the just as with the unjust: Far be it from you. Shall the Judge of all the earth not do right? What are vehement and strong assertions, as certain and undoubted, if these are not? He knew for certain, then, both that God cannot appoint anything iniquitous, and that it is not just before God as judge that the just and the unjust be damned alike; and so he begged this one thing—not only that God should not damn the just for the sake of the unjust, which seemed to him too alien from God's justice, but that for the sake of a few just he should spare even the unjust, or at least the place or city itself, which seemed not unworthy of God's highest goodness. For the matter was not about any chastisement whatever, but about judicial punishment, and in a manner eternal: of which kind of punishment it is certain the just are never punished for the sake of the unjust.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: GAR rigor/equity & Jer 31; PLAC two parts; tip before Quarto king
english: GAR. 3. Since God, in executing his judgments, sometimes acts from the rigor of justice, sometimes tempers justice with equity, I say Abraham, for his charity toward the Sodomites, earnestly desired that God would temper that judgment with some testimony of mercy: and so, setting aside for now God's more rigorous mode, he clung only to the ordinary and more common dispensation of divine justice—especially since that covenant lately struck with him in Gen. 17 sat deep in his mind, namely the covenant of grace, in which God promised he would not impute others' sins, Jer. 31:29–30. And of which covenant he sometimes shows some sweetness even to those who do not belong to it. PLAC. There are two parts of Abraham's speech: one asserts that it does not agree with God's justice that the just perish with the wicked; the other asks of God that for the sake of a few just he spare the city—which, I confess, would not be looked for as due, but rather as a testimony of mercy: so this part does not serve the matter we are treating. From that other part our argument is drawn, which agrees not only with equity but also with the rigor of justice in every respect. So what this reply aims at, and what new thing it brings to my argument, I see none. I will only reply this: If in the covenant of grace God promised he would not impute others' sins, then he does not impute to us Adam's first actual sin: How then does he punish us for that sin, namely by inflicting a judicial penalty—original corruption? For the rest I do not deny that God sometimes involves the pious in the same temporal condemnation with the impious; for no one is so pious and just that he does not sometimes sin, and the pious do not, as they ought, detest, flee, and rebuke the sins of those among whom they are mixed. Meanwhile, however, calamities of this kind become for the pious paternal chastisements by which it is provided that they not perish eternally with the impious. But we in this cause are treating of judicial imputation and damnation to penalties properly so called and satisfactory to justice—such as those the law threatens and justice, that it may be satisfied, exacts—which innocents, least of all as sureties of the guiltless, we contend with Abraham's testimony clash with God's justice and equity when borne for others' sins.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: Quarto — king implants rebellion then imputes and strips virtues
english: Fourth, suppose there is some King endowed with such power that he can, if he wishes, inject into his subjects a spirit of rebellion and disobedience. Do you think that if he is wise, if just, if good, he would be so disposed that to those who would otherwise be faithful in that city he would first impute the crime of rebels, then, to punish it, strip them of justice and fidelity and the other virtues, so that thereafter they could not but be themselves rebels and criminals?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: Quarto close — do not foster such thoughts of God
english: Do not, then, I beg you, dearest brother in Christ, foster such thoughts about God, which to me at least certainly strike horror. Fifth and finally, let the Apostle's words to Gal. 6:5 help us: Each will bear his own burden. And to Rom. 14:12: Each of us will give account of himself to God.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: Quinto — Gal 6:5 / Rom 14:12; account for Adam's act?
english: Do you think that on that day account must be rendered by all and each of us for Adam's actual sin? Have not wills, faculties, actions, and gifts been attributed by God to each of us as our own? Of these indeed account will certainly have to be rendered by each of us; of Adam's action, perpetrated some thousands of years before we began to exist, account will not be owed by us, but by Adam himself before God.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: PLAC — head's rebellion pervading nature is imputed
english: For the rest, the extreme words of this comparison of yours, and of the chapter, if they are well understood, I approve: this rebellion of the head by which it pervaded the whole nature is attributed and imputed to all men.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: natural efficiency infects posterity; tip before Cap. VIII
english: Namely, Adam's actual rebellion itself by natural efficiency sowed its own seed and virus into all Adam's faculties and fixed it deep in the marrow, and that evil crept, and by natural generation spread and propagated itself, and by its contagion infected all posterity. Therefore, since it is in each human being, it is deservedly attributed and imputed to them.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: open — reply to OT arguments for imputing Adam's actual sin
english: CHAPTER VIII. Reply to the arguments which for the Imputation of Adam's Actual sin are drawn from the Old Testament, Cap. V. The status of the question having been constituted and illustrated as it seemed good to you, at length, most distinguished Sir, in the fifth chapter of your treatise you draw the forces of your arguments into the field and unfold them. And first of all there come forth a few drawn from the Old Testament.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: first — tree interdict syllogism; conclusion conceded
english: The first breaks out from the interdict of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and proceeds thus. If that interdict, you say, and the threat looked not only to the first parents but also to the whole human race, it follows that the transgression of that Command made not only the first parents liable to death, but also the whole human race. But the prior is true. Therefore the latter also. The first part of the major (which concerns the interdict) is outside controversy: for who will deny that the Lord gave the law not only to Adam but also to all posterity? Who will deny that by that law eating of that fruit was forbidden to all men? And the consequence is manifest from the event: for when the interdict was violated, both Adam and all posterity were made liable to death. At the outset I concede the conclusion of this argument of yours: for it is friendly to my opinion as well as to yours. I believe firmly with you that Adam's transgression made not only the first parents liable to death, but also the whole human race. But the question between us is only about the mode by which that transgression made the whole human race liable to death.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: mode only — opponent's immediate imputation vs natural efficiency
english: You ascribe this to God's justice, which immediately imputes that transgression, cut off from the corruption that followed, to us all, by this very fact that we are sons of Adam, not otherwise than if we ourselves, who then were nothing, had committed it, and consequently punishes us first with inflicted moral corruption which is sin and the cause of all our sins, then with death of the body and eternal death. So you want that actual transgression to have made us liable to death by the intervention of such imputation. But I say without such imputation that that transgression by natural efficiency and sequel vitiated Adam's faculties, even that by which he begot us, and that those vitiated faculties begot vitiated offspring, and this another, and so the vice, propagated and multiplied together with human nature, reached all men, Christ alone excepted, by the sole law of nature whereby each thing begets its like—which general law, belonging not only to men but also to other Creatures endowed with the faculty of generating, and set and sanctioned by the antecedent decree concerning creating the world and constituting nature, it did not become God to abrogate or infringe because of Adam's transgression.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: Thomas praised; inherent vice; status questionis restated
english: So I praise these words of Thomas Aquinas. In each of us there is truly and properly sin deep in the marrow, not indeed actual, but, so to speak, habitual, worthy not only of temporal death but of eternal also, which our side usually prove against the Papists with many arguments which you have doubtless both read and approve. We, therefore, Adam's transgression made liable to bodily and eternal death by the intervention of the inherent vice and fault with which it infected us. But this vice in Adam natural sequel produced; and from Adam into us it was propagated no otherwise than human nature itself by carnal generation. I wanted to repeat the status of the question in this place, because it becomes us to keep it purged and clarified perpetually before our eyes, lest sometime straying from it we slide into empty logomachies.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: premises need times-distinction; positive law may be temporary
english: Although I admit the conclusion of this syllogism of yours, yet the premises are not so clear that they do not need some distinction useful to the matter we are treating. For how, I ask, do you understand these propositions—that the Lord gave that law not only to Adam but also to all posterity; that by that law eating of that fruit was forbidden to men? Times certainly must be distinguished. For if Adam had begotten children in paradise, that interdict would have bound them after they had been born—unless perhaps God at last abrogated that interdict; for who knows the mind of the Lord? It was a positive law, fencing Adam's freedom of choice about a thing indifferent by its own nature, and so could be prescribed for a time and, that time elapsed, abrogated, just as the laws about choice of foods which God once laid down for his people. Who of us can know whether God had willed that interdict to be in force forever, or only for some certain time, which being finished, and man's obedience amply proved, he would have taken away, man being given freedom thereafter to use that tree? For it does not become us to break into God's secrets, or confidently to assert what we do not know.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: binds posterity when existing, not before; tip before Hypognosticon
english: I concede freely, however, that it would have bound Adam's posterity at the time they existed; but that at the time they did not exist they were then bound to observe it I can in no way concede. Nature's own law, from which no one can be exempted, does not bind to obedience except those who are in the nature of things, and as long as they are in the nature of things. Those who have not yet entered into the World are not yet held to observe laws laid down for those who are in the World. The Israelites once received the law in the desert for themselves and their posterity; who would believe that at that time, while they were wandering in the same desert, David, or the Virgin Mary, already then owed to observe that law? Or that therefore the sins of those who first received the law were to be imputed to all posterity even to the consummation of the ages?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: infant in utero — future sins not imputed; contradiction
english: Do you think those sins are imputed to an infant in the mother's womb which, if it had lived and reached old age, it would have done through the whole time of life? I do not think so. Why then do you want an actual sin imputed to it that was then committed when it did not yet exist—indeed some thousands of years before it was—and which it itself committed neither in act nor in potency: not in act, because it was not; not in potency, because when it was being committed it could not then be—this is what I mean: it could not be with respect to that time in which that sin was perpetrated—so far that it implies a contradiction that that same numbered deed which you want imputed to us was done by us, or was done. We never did it, nor could we do it, nor since we were born can we do it.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: Hypognosticon — God does not punish infant for unlived time
english: Finely the author of the Hypognosticon Against the Pelagians—whether he is Augustine or another: God, he says, foreknowing its evil works which it was going to do in perfect age, said of his people that it would perish. Is it so, mad Pelagian—is God who is just in all his ways and holy in all his works to be believed, for such a reason, to judge an uncircumcised little child so as to punish him as a doer for crimes not done, to impute some time where life was not lived, where willing and nilling were not of the will? Far be this before a just judge, and so on. See how greatly the pious man abhors that thought—that God imputes to a little child some time where life was not lived, although it could have lived—and how much he judges that not to agree with God's justice.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: a fortiori never-could-live; interdict silence on posterity
english: What then would he say of that time when the little child not only was not living life, but could not even live; and of a sin which it not only did not do, but never could do? But if by the Apostle's example in the Epistles to the Galatians and to the Hebrews we wish carefully to weigh Scripture's words and silence, what reason is there why we should not observe that in the Interdict, in the sentence pronounced to Adam after the interdict was violated, no mention of posterity was made? God already then took care, to be sure, lest he should offer you any handle for sensing concerning his justice as you do.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: even if bound when nonexistent — obeyed; ate in Adam not in us
english: But grant that that interdict bound us to obedience for that time when we did not yet exist, when Adam alone was in paradise with his wife—what did it require of us? That we should not eat of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil? We obeyed: for those who at that time could not eat certainly did not eat. We ate, you will say, in Adam. Well and good: therefore we did not eat in ourselves. Since therefore in one Adam we ate that fruit, it was fitting that we also be punished in one Adam: and since we did not eat in our own persons, we ought not to have been punished in our own persons.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: interdict vs threat — as Adam only, or as distinct persons?
english: I should like to know how the interdict looked to us—whether insofar as we are persons distinct from Adam's person, or only insofar as we were nothing other than Adam himself? For then certainly no part of us existed, indeed not even the seed from which we were begotten, indeed not even the seed from which our hundredth parent sprang. You will not say the former. If you affirm the latter, what reason is there why the interdict should not have looked to us, with respect to that time, except insofar as we were nothing but Adam himself—yet you want the threat joined to the interdict to look to us insofar as we are persons diverse and separate from Adam? For my part I do not understand why the interdict should pertain to us in one way, the threat in another.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: event reply — Adam for ban, posterity for inherent vice; tip
english: But you argue from the event. For this—when the interdict was violated, both Adam and all posterity were made liable to death. Certainly: but Adam immediately for the interdict violated by himself, posterity for the vice and sin which, propagated from Adam, inheres in each.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: sentence syllogism — if penalty common, sin common
english: You go on and draw an argument from the sentence which God pronounced to Adam fallen into sin in these words, because you obeyed your wife's voice, and ate from the tree, and so on. From there you argue thus: If the penalty was common, the sin ought also to have been common. But the penalty was common. Therefore the sin also. You prove the major by this syllogism: A just Judge does not inflict a common penalty on all men except for a sin common to all. It occurs to your mind that this whole can be conceded by me, who acknowledge a sin common to all men, namely hereditary vice worthy of common penalties.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: hereditary vice conceded; missing third — natural propagation
english: So you press further. Now, you say, I assume that first sin which sentenced all men to penalty is common to all, either by their own act, or by imputation: Not by their own act, because Adam alone actually sinned. Therefore by imputation, because namely it is imputed to all. Why did you omit the third member so greatly sung against the Pelagians—or by natural propagation? For it is established that the first sin passed into us (not as it was a transient action, but as it was aversion from God and conversion to creatures as to the ultimate end, remaining in Adam)—passed, I say, not by an imputation which is outside us, but by true communication and propagation.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: first sin by communication not external imputation; common penalties
english: For this sin common to all, common penalties are inflicted on all: not indeed satisfactory ones in this life, at least with respect to the faithful, but penalties nonetheless: There is inflicted also, unless the grace of Christ intervene, a satisfactory penalty, but one which never finishes satisfaction—eternal death. I therefore between the act of the first sin and imputation interpose in all Adam's posterity hereditary corruption which is imputed to us unto those penalties.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: proximate cause in us — why impute alien actual sin?
english: Why do you seek so far the proximate cause of the evils which we all suffer, when it meets you near at hand? Why do you seek it in Adam when in each of us it shows itself? Why is it needful that God impute to us an alien sin, when in us he finds a sin which merits those penalties? Why should he impute an actual sin which we did neither in act nor in potency, when he sees in each of us a vice actually inhering, worthy of those penalties?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: mediate imputation via shared viciousness; three in order
english: You will perhaps reply that the miseries of this life and the death of the body were inflicted on Adam for actual sin, because, God says, you obeyed your wife's voice and ate from the tree which I commanded you, saying, and so on. And so you will gather: whose sin's penalties we pay, that sin is ours. We pay the penalties of Adam's actual sin. It is ours, therefore; how, unless by imputation? What if I concede (as I did in constituting the status of the question) that Adam's sin is imputed to us and is ours, but only mediately; because by participation in the viciousness which he left in Adam we communicate with him, and by the habitual depravity of will derived from him we consent to him? For these three follow one another in order: Adam's actual sin, the corruption inhering in us, the penalty. This is born proximately from the corruption inhering in us; the corruption from Adam's actual sin. Reread, if you please, the words of Aegidius Hunnius which I wrote down in Cap. 2 while constituting the status of the question, and also of Chamier, whose place I noted there.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: proximate vs mediate poena; tip before personal sentence words
english: Formally also I answer the premises by this distinction: Whose sin's penalties we pay proximately, or immediately—That sin is ours. I concede. But whose sin's penalties we pay only mediately, another sin namely intervening—that sin is ours: I deny. For it is enough if it is the cause of our sin. For you know that worn saying in the schools: what is the cause of the cause is also the cause of the caused. But that we pay the penalties of the actual sin proximately—I deny; Mediately—I concede. Therefore it is our sin does not follow; but well, it is the cause of our sin.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: quia paruisti — words personal to Adam, not to us immediately
english: What then? Do you think those words—because you obeyed your wife's voice—were spoken to you, to your person, I say, and look to you immediately? Do you not see how personal it was, and proper to Adam, that he was Eve's husband, how fitted to his person these words are? Could God's sentence have been conceived in words more, so to speak, personal, more proper to Adam's person, less common to the human race?

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: sentence most personal; if immediate imputation, common words
english: But do not think that was done by him rashly. If God had imputed that actual sin of Adam to humans not yet existing, and by his sentence had immediately adjudged them all to those penalties for that sin, with what wisdom would he have conceived a common sentence in common words, and such as could be applied to all and each human, or would he have injected some mention of Adam's posterity.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: penalties via Adam's communicated malice; leaven of the mass
english: But now he did the Contrary—to what end, unless that we understand the penalties decreed by that sentence do not pertain to us, except because Adam communicated them with us, the malice of his sin which merits them having been communicated through carnal generation? and so that we should not seek the cause why we pay those penalties in God imputing to us an action which we in no way committed, that he may punish us, but in Adam alone, and in the nature of the sin itself, which, like some leaven put into the mass of the human race, corrupted that whole mass not through God's imputation but through carnal generation, and infected it with malice. You see that I am pleading God's cause; do not, I beg you, oppose him.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: conscience recoils — God punishing infants by bare imputation
english: For it vehemently offends me that you, and certain other brothers of ours, say that God punishes all humans, even little children, with death of the body (and eternal), indeed with death of the soul, which formally is sin, for an actual sin which is theirs in no way, except by imputation, because God imputes it to them. Conscience shudders even to think it, and that he may give you and them another mind, I earnestly beg the Lord from the heart.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: Bellarmine — by what right? imputation alone makes common
english: For by what right, as Bellarmine says somewhere (with whom this cause is common with you), is what is not mine imputed to me? What is this justice—by imputing to make common to all a sin which otherwise is not common to all, and therefore to punish all humans so severely? That first sin, you say, is not common to all except by imputation, because namely it is imputed to all. Therefore, I say, before it is imputed to all, it is not common to all. What therefore is common to all must be credited to that imputation alone, which namely is God's judicial act.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: false unjust imputation; tip before Gospel-promise argument
english: Consider, I beg you, what a false and unjust imputation would be, if this is not; And whether an action befits God which makes us sinners who otherwise were not sinners, and indeed formally, and of itself, and whether this is not to refer the cause of all our sins and evils to God; and give glory to your creator and redeemer. Call back to mind what I said in Cap. 3 of this examination § III. And do not think that opinion of yours was drawn and deduced from the fountains either of the ancient fathers, or of those who first and chiefly set hand to reforming the Church in the last century. Far otherwise did they think, as, God granting, I shall make plain in another Chapter. For now it is enough for me to untie the knots of your arguments.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: Gospel promise — seed of woman; common remedy ≠ imputation
english: You add that the same is demonstrated from the promise of the Gospel inserted there in verse 15 concerning the seed of the woman, Christ namely the avenger of the human race, who will crush the serpent's head. Just as from a common penalty it is inferred that the sin was common, so from a common Remedy for blotting out that sin it follows that that sin was common to all. But I confess a first common sin, yet seated not in the imputation of Adam's actual sin, but in corruption implanted in all; and made common not by divine imputation, but by carnal generation.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: else Devil one, God the rest; remedy needs faith-consent
english: Otherwise the Devil by his temptation would have made a single human a sinner, God (thinking it I wholly shudder) by that imputation of his all the rest; of which imputation show if you can either the necessity or the justice. For the rest, however common the remedy may be, yet it is not applied, not imputed to any adult, except to one consenting and apprehending it by faith, nor is it ours except by the gift of Christ and of God. But that Adam's actual sin should be given to us by God—far be it that I believe.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: imputation before consent — remedy overturns your view
english: But you want the imputation of Adam's actual sin to precede all our consent, whether habitual or actual. Therefore this common remedy rather overturns your opinion than confirms it.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: serpent as cause of common evil — not the evil itself
english: What of this—that it even supplies me arms fatal to that imputation of yours? For I reason thus. That against which a common remedy is set is either the common evil itself or the cause why the evil is common. In this place the common remedy is set against the serpent; and the serpent is not itself the common evil. Therefore the serpent is the cause why the evil is common.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: poison-spread vs imputation — imputation is God's work
english: But he is not the cause of a common evil unless either he himself breathed that evil into all, or at least produced in one such an evil as of itself, by its own natural force, spread and propagated itself into all like poison, like a plague. Imputation, the infliction of penalty, is God's work, not the ancient serpent's.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: if only by imputation, evil's community not from serpent; tip
english: If therefore actual sin is not common to all except by imputation—because God imputes it to all—and original sin or inhering vice is not in us except because it is fixed in us by God as the penalty of that imputed actual, the community of evil is not from the serpent. Nor is that privation of original justice and hereditary corruption the serpent's virus which he breathed upon us, but (which my mind shudders to say) God's effect and work.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: death-reply — Devil causes sin that merits death by nature
english: You will perhaps say that death is the Devil's work, which yet sin follows by the intervention of divine imputation and judgment. Namely, because the Devil is the cause of a sin which of itself and by its nature merits death, and which cannot fail to be imputed to the one in whom, or by whom, it is, unless satisfaction intervene.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: Adam's first actual not by nature owed to all as corrupting imputation
english: But that first actual sin of Adam, whose author the serpent himself was, did not by its nature merit the moral corruption of all humans, nor was it by its nature of such a kind that, divine justice being preserved, it could not but be imputed to all humans unto fixing that vice in them. And if you think it was such by nature, you will also depart from the opinion of the great men who with you defend that imputation, and you will do us a great favor if you teach and prove it.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: Ps 32:1–2 — no lynx-eye sees immediate Adam-imputation there
english: Your second Argument you carve out from Ps. 32:1–2. Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered: Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed iniquity—by an art which I may admire more than follow. For what eye of the mind, however lynx-keen, could see in those words the immediate imputation of Adam's actual sin to the whole posterity? You nevertheless try with many words to make me see it with you in them, but I cannot. Would that you had rewoven the force of your argument in applied syllogistic form, and not buried it under a great abundance of words; from which I cannot dig it out.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: grant non-imputation beatitude; contested origin-vice as proper penalty
english: The Psalmist testifies in general that one is blessed to whom sin is not imputed—namely, what one either committed or has in oneself; but which sin can rightly be imputed to us, or not imputed, he does not teach. You prove that one to whom sin is imputed is miserable: I concede. You add, if this is true in general of every sin, it is true also of original sin, which we contracted in Adam, and which seems to have had to be said from Adam. I concede this too. You subjoin that that vice of origin is the penalty of the first parents' first sin; and that, since you understand penalty properly so called, is the very thing which is in question between us.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: anomia / blessed–miserable chain; unspoken minor we are not blessed
english: You say the names by which the Psalmist called sins can signify that first rebellion of Adam, namely no less than Cain's murder, or the Israelite people's rebellion. You add that it is anomia, which word the Apostle used in citing this place: Be it so; what follows from that I do not yet understand: for the same may be said of Cain's murder, of the crime of Sodom, of Absalom's incest and rebellion, and finally of any other crime of anyone. But you yourself conclude something; let us hear you then. From there, you say, we ought to conclude according to the Apostle using the Prophet's words, that he is blessed to whom sins are not imputed, and consequently that he is miserable to whom sins are imputed, and since our whole misery is from Adam's first sin, if that sin is imputed to us, we are miserable, if on the contrary it is not imputed to us, we are blessed. You left us, I think, the minor to be subsumed: But we are not blessed: Therefore that sin is imputed to us.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: form fails; tip before Abraham justification proof
english: I pass over that the matter of this argument of yours, because of the multitude of terms, does not admit syllogistic form. I pass over that the same can be said of any other sin—if it is imputed to us, we are miserable. I say that for us to be blessed, the non-imputation of some one sin is not enough, but that of all is required. I say it contributes to my beatitude not if some sin is not imputed to me—say Judas's incest—but if that is not imputed to me by grace which could be imputed to me from justice. But I deny that the first actual sin can be imputed to us from justice. I say finally that our whole misery is from Adam's first sin, not because it is proximately imputed to us, but because it is the cause of that sin which, because it is in us, and therefore is ours, can be imputed to us from justice.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: Abraham justified by faith — no path to Adam-imputation
english: To firm this reason of yours you cite the Apostle's reasoning proving that Abraham was justified because he believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness. Who would ever have hoped that from there it could be effected that Adam's first actual sin is immediately imputed to all humans, and indeed unto this penalty, namely hereditary corruption? For this is our question, whose affirmation was formally to be concluded by you. You must indeed be subtle, and a wondrous craftsman of arguments, who can fashion that imputation from places of this kind.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: contrary rule granted; deny Adam's actual as formal sinner-maker
english: But what do you conclude from there? (for to transfer all your words hither would be laborious, and not necessary.) Just as, then, you say, a man is justified and blessed because he believes in him who justifies the ungodly; and his faith is imputed to him for righteousness without works, because sin is not imputed, it follows by the rule of contraries that a man is damned and miserable who does not believe in God, because sin is imputed to him unto condemnation. I concede. You add, and in general every sin which he committed. I admit. You subjoin, and in species this sin of Adam, which constitutes him a sinner. This I now deny, if, as is fair, by Adam's sin you understand his actual sin, and also immediate imputation.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: Chamier — Adam constitutes sinners causally, not formally
english: For that (as most learned Chamier has it) constitutes us sinners not formally, but causally; of which matter in its place. These alone you found in the Old Testament by which you thought that imputation could be concluded. I could also have propped my replies with the authority of great Theologians, and from the same places drawn forth other arguments hostile to yours: but I consult brevity, and I do not wish to weary you as reader with too great a flood of arguments.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: visiting fathers' iniquity — unfit to prove unlimited Adam-imputation
english: The places in which God is said to visit the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons are not even commemorated here: for you saw that they are more fitted for defending against my arguments than for proving the imputation of Adam's actual sin. For in truth no argument can be made from them which does not proceed equally of Adam's other sins as of the first, and of our other parents' sins as of Adam's: and that limitation to the fourth generation openly resists an unlimited imputation to all generations: and that other limitation in those who hate me presupposes hatred of God in those who are visited: whereas the imputation of the first actual sin presupposes no vice in infants, but, if you are believed, makes it. But of these places elsewhere.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: if dogma true, revealed in OT — but nowhere revealed
english: Now I may argue thus. If the dogma of the imputation of Adam's first actual sin to all and each human is true and to be believed, it is surely revealed somewhere in the Old Testament. But it is revealed nowhere in the Old Testament. Therefore it is not true and to be believed. The minor is clear from this our dispute. I prove the major, because the law is fitted to detect and lay open sin: through the law is knowledge of sin. But it does not discharge this its office as it ought, if it does not lay open that sin which is common to all humans, which is the cause of all others, whence the condemnation of all humans hangs. But it does not lay it open according to your opinion, who will have a sin of that kind be Adam's first actual sin imputed to all humans, unless this imputation can be gathered from the law, or the Old Testament.

title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: law detects sin; judicial imputation needs a law; tip Cap. IX
english: Next, if that actual sin is proximately imputed to all, and humans are bound to believe it, that imputation rests on some law, by whose help it must also be known, and that a very ancient one. Since therefore no such law occurs in the Old Testament, it must be confessed that there is no such imputation. Finally unbelieving Israelites who died before Christ's coming were judged according to the law which they received from God by the hand of Moses. But according to the law they could not be damned immediately for Adam's actual sin, nor could it be imputed to them, unless according to the law it could be established that that sin was the sin of each of them. The same must be said of all other humans. For every judicial imputation of sin and infliction of penalty is according to some law. But the immediate imputation of actual sin to all humans and the infliction of inhering vice, if, as you say, it is, is surely judicial. Therefore it is according to some law. Produce that law, then, if you can. None certainly can be found in any place of Scripture.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: open — NT reply; Rom 5:12ff only possible locus
english: CHAPTER IX. Reply to the Arguments which for the immediate imputation of the first actual sin to all humans are drawn from the New Testament. You next provoke with arguments sought from the New Testament, and from nowhere else than from Rom. 5:12 and following. Indeed if there is any place in all Scripture from which the immediate imputation of the first actual sin to the whole human race could be made out, this is surely the one.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: keep hereditary-vice hypothesis or drop Rom 5 proofs
english: Yet I do not see by what pact it can be elicited, this hypothesis being set—that from Adam's first sin there passed into all humans by carnal generation a vice which is truly sin, sufficient for damning the human race. And so I hold that either the arguments drawn from that chapter, or this hypothesis, which all the churches of the Protestants have hitherto held most constantly, must be renounced.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: deferred replies / three chapters of human testimonies
english: But by what counsel it was done by you, I do not know: that when in the Theses I went to meet the arguments which are drawn from Rom. 5, and proposed to you all my replies to be run through and refuted, you yet relegated them to chapter IX of your treatise with no mention at all of them made in this place where you treat those arguments, three chapters even being interposed between them and this treatment of yours, by which you try to crush my opinion with human testimonies.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: truth needs no art; commentary confuses the status
english: If room is to be given to conjecture, you wished by that means to occupy and fortify the minds of readers, lest they be wounded by the stings of my replies and reasons. In which, if this was your counsel, you seem to me to have distrusted and hurt your cause. For truth does not desire an art of this kind; simple, open, ingenuous, candid, even when it is humble, it breathes something noble, where (in which it is stronger than every thing) and trusting the God of truth it then most rejoices and shines and gleams, when it is compared with its contrary, however painted. But that, whether it was done by you with that counsel or another, disturbs our dispute, and scatters it, and forces much to be repeated.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: unus≠primus vs one-man/one-man Adam–Christ; follow your method
english: To this is added that in this place you seem to me to write a commentary rather than to knit syllogisms: and not to have before your eyes the status of the controversy well constituted and purged; for you often confuse what most ought to be distinguished, and you also mix in certain things which, though true in themselves, yet do not look hither—such as that which you observe, and prove by some examples, that among the Hebrews 'one' is often taken for 'first.' For that it cannot so be taken in this place is opposed by the opposition which the Apostle sets between one man and one man, that Adam and this Christ. Likewise between one trespass and one gift: not to mention that the Apostle's aim demands that unity in this place be opposed to plurality: but it does not help to digress. It would therefore have been better, as I at least judge, that what you wished to be cut apart and disjoined in places should, for the sake of avoiding either tedious repetition or inconvenient distraction, be brought together into this place, and set before the reader's eyes at once in one coherent context of speech; but because it seemed otherwise to you, I will accommodate my method to yours, and will follow you foot by foot, and will weigh those arguments which you could gather from Rom. 5, my Theses having been rejected into another place.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: Rom 5:12 — sin entered; deny both members; tip before four proofs
english: You begin from verse 12. It runs thus: through one man sin entered into the world, through sin death, and so death passed upon all men, because all sinned. So the place stands: now let us shake it out. If any argument of that imputation lies hidden in it, that will doubtless fall out either from the words 'sin entered into the world,' or from the following 'through sin death,' or from these eph' ho, or finally from the word 'sinned.' From those words, 'sin entered into the world,' whichever way you turn yourself, you will not elicit anything except this: If by the sin which entered into the world Adam's first actual sin must be understood, and actual sin could not enter into all humans otherwise than by imputation, the consequence is that Adam's first actual sin is imputed to all humans. But the prior is true; Therefore the latter also. I deny both members of the antecedent.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: opponent obscures — original mixed with Adam's actual
english: You prove the prior, namely that by the sin which entered into the world Adam's first actual sin must be understood, but you add (which obscures your mind) that that sin transfused into us is called original: And soon, that original sin in us is from it: Likewise, that Adam by begetting transfused into us a corruption which we call original sin. And a little later, that this sin was indeed committed by Adam himself, but that by guilt and reatus it passed into us by imputation, And so in him was actual and personal, but in us is called original. Thus you sometimes confuse original sin with Adam's actual sin, sometimes distinguish, and sometimes mix Adam's actual sin with origin's corruption; sometimes you separate it from it.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: speak distinctly — one original or two? Pighius vs churches
english: Speak, I beg and ask you, more distinctly and more clearly: for nothing so hinders the investigation of truth as either ambiguity of speech, or the inconstancy and slipperiness of speech of the one with whom you have to do. If, as some do, you believe two original sins, one imputed, the other inhering in us, why nowhere do you say that openly? If you believe only one, say constantly, either with Pighius that it is Adam's actual sin imputed to us all, or with the confession of faith of our Churches that it is hereditary corruption, or inhering vice: and do not mix or crush those two which according to your opinion stand a maximum interval apart from each other.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: actual past vs inhering vice — before four proofs
english: Adam's first actual sin, committed some five thousand years ago, has passed, and did not remain in the nature of things: inhering vice remained with human nature, and is and thrives today. That is unique in number; of this there are as many individuals as there are humans. That was an action; this stands in the manner of a habit. That is outside us, and it is not possible for it to be in us; this is within us, sticking in us. That you think is ours, but only by God's imputation; this is truly ours, deeply inhering in us: That you will have as fault; this as its penalty. With this ambiguity and confusion removed, let us see by what reasons you prove that the Apostle by the sin which entered into the world understands Adam's actual sin. Which was certainly Pighius's opinion, which Bellarmine himself refuted with some arguments, but I do not wish to press you with prejudices.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: proof 1 — through one man ≠ Adam's actual named
english: You use, as far as I can gather, four arguments. 1. By one man the Apostle understands the first man, namely Adam. Therefore by the sin which entered into the World through one man he understands Adam's first actual sin. I deny that it follows. For the Apostle does not say Adam's sin, but that through Adam sin entered into the World. He considers Adam as the cause of this sin, the World—that is, humans—as the subject: nor did he wish to teach who first sinned in the World (for Eve before Adam, and before her the devil, sinned) but that through Adam the corruption of sin was introduced into all humans.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: proof 2 — infected formally vs causally
english: 2. The Apostle treats of the sin which infected the World and brought in death. But this fits only Adam's actual sin from which original sin is in us. Therefore the Apostle treats only of Adam's actual sin. I distinguish the sin which infected the World: for it is said to have infected either formally, or causally or efficiently. In the former way inhering vice and corruption infected the world; in the latter Adam's actual sin. But the Apostle in this verse speaks of the sin which infected the world in the former way: for he does not say that sin infected the world, but that it entered into the world. Adam's actual sin is said to have infected the world causally, because it is the cause of that sin which entered into the world. But the sin which entered into the world, since it is inside the world, formally affects and infects that in which it is.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: proofs 3–4 — article & names; tip before name-distinctions
english: 3. He hamartia with the article designates a certain individual of sin, so much so that scarcely in Paul do you find ten hamartian with the article added declaring anything else, as the most learned interpreters note. Therefore it does not designate hereditary corruption, which is not one individual of sin, but Adam's actual sin. I deny the antecedent. I remember reading no interpreter who observes that the name hamartia with the prefixed article signifies among Paul a certain individual of sin or some singular sin one in number: on the contrary they observe that almost everywhere it designates that hereditary corruption which is in all humans from birth. Your fourth reason finally is sought from other names by which you think the Apostle marked this sin which entered into the world. What in the following verses the Apostle calls parabasis, transgression, paraptoma, a fall or defection, parakoe, disobedience—that is Adam's actual sin. But this sin which entered into the world the Apostle calls parabasis, paraptoma, and parakoe. Therefore this sin which entered into the world is Adam's actual sin.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: Respondeo — παράπτωμα vs other names; deny major/minor
english: I answer that the name paraptoma must be distinguished from the other two: For by that one the Apostle sometimes designates Adam's sin, sometimes the vice arisen from Adam's sin in all humans: By these he signifies only Adam's sin, not indeed the actual cut off from the habitual, but together with the habitual. And so as far as this name paraptoma is concerned, I deny the Major: but as far as the other two, I deny the minor.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: three names ≠ actual cut from Adam's corruption
english: Next I deny that the Apostle by any of those three names designated Adam's actual sin cut off from the corruption which it produced in Adam, although yet this our controversy must be understood of actual sin so cut off. For you will have it that by that actual sin of his Adam earned that corruption both for himself and for us. You cannot therefore prove that by hamartia in this place Adam's actual sin must be understood.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: even if actual — entered by venom, not imputation
english: Grant nevertheless that it is so understood; I will deny that that sin entered into the world by imputation. Rather it is said to have entered into the world, because he left his venom in Adam, which without that kind of imputation crept from Adam into Seth, from Seth into Enosh, from him into Kenan, and so little by little flowed from father into sons, until it reached us by natural propagation and multiplication.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: Sustinui — imputation must be in Scripture, here if anywhere
english: I have sustained your assault; see whether you can sustain mine. For from here rises for me an argument overturning your opinion. You will certainly grant me that dogma concerning the imputation of Adam's actual sin to the whole human race, if it is true, if it must be believed, is taught somewhere in Scripture, the most absolute norm of our faith. You will also grant that, if it is taught anywhere, it is taught in this place, where the Apostle accurately explains whatever evil flowed from Adam into the human race. You will grant at last that whatever evils Adam communicated with his posterity, those the Apostle reduces to these two, sin and death.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: your actual-to-penalties vs my hereditary vice
english: Let us see therefore which sin he understands. You will have it to be Adam's actual sin imputed to all humans unto two penalties, the privation of original righteousness or original vice, and death. I say it is original vice or hereditary corruption inhering in individual humans, but not Adam's actual sin immediately imputed to individual humans. Your opinion the reasons you brought do not prove: for to them, as you see, I have replied.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: Placeus syllogism; Beza ἡ ἁμαρτία; tip before GAR
english: I prove mine thus. If any sin the Apostle teaches in Rom. 5. was communicated by Adam with all humans, that certainly is what he teaches entered into the world through Adam, and through it death, so that death passed through unto all humans. But that sin which he teaches entered into the world through Adam, and through it death, is hereditary corruption, not however Adam's actual sin taken precisely. Therefore if the Apostle teaches any sin, as he truly does, communicated by Adam with all humans, that certainly is hereditary corruption, not however Adam's actual sin. You will not deny the Major: for it is manifest. Certainly the sin through which he says death entered into the world, that is, as he himself exposes, and you after him, into all humans, is that to which he nearest ascribes the death and condemnation of the human race. I prove the Minor. The first reason the very name of sin he hamartia supplies me: for so (as the most learned Beza noted on this verse) the Apostle is accustomed to call that hereditary disease: so much so that scarcely in Paul with the article added does it declare anything else. But a hereditary disease is not Adam's actual sin, but corruption, and vice arisen from it.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — articular ἡ ἁμαρτία not always original sin
english: GAR. Although the Apostle more often designates original sin, inhering in the entrails of humans, by the name he hamartia, it is nevertheless not necessary that wherever he uses that word, that sin be understood: which anyone will easily recognize who has read Paul speaking of sin, Rom. VI. 2. 6. 23: 2. Cor. 15. 56: 2. Thess. 2. 3. Heb. XII. 4.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — first reason is Beza's; Calvin/Martyr; silence
english: PLAC. This my first reason is not mine, but of a most great man, Beza, whom the learned man strikes through my side. See if you will his Annot. on Rom. 5. 12. By sin in that place I understand what Calvin, Beza, Martyr, and other theologians of first note of that kind understood, from whom the rest, who accuse me of innovated doctrine, depart: which lest it lie open, mention of Beza, and his words, from which the nerve and strength of the argument hung, (so much so that scarcely in Paul with the article added does it declare anything else,) the learned man passed by in deep silence.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — usual articular sense; examples confirm
english: For I do not argue from this, that by that name hamartia the Apostle designates inhering sin, but that so often, that scarcely ever with the article added does it declare anything else, and here the article is added. But who does not know that the most usual signification is to be preferred to the rarest, unless perhaps a grave reason blocks it, which here appears none, or is brought forward by the learned man. Nay, the examples he brings confirm our reason rather than overturn it: for in those places by the name of sin inhering vice either alone, or with its fruits, is understood.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR ἀχώριστα; PLAC — remission lifts imputation
english: GAR. 2. Since the imputation of the first sin, and hereditary corruption, are inseparable, even here we do not deny that by the name of sin, by force of consequence, that corruption can be understood. PLAC. If they were inseparable, as long as corruption remains, so long would imputation remain: which fights with the opinion of all theologians, as many as are not Pelagians. For imputation is taken away by the remission of original sin, which is done, not so that it may not be, but so that it may no longer be imputed. But if by the name of the sin which entered into the world through one man hereditary corruption is understood, by what argument will those who oppose us in this cause prove that actual sin is understood which was not made ours except by imputation? For that inhering sin must be understood, and the name hamartia with the article, both the authority of the greatest theologians, and the adversaries' confession, sufficiently confirm.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC second reason — εἰς τὸν κόσμον = all humans
english: A second reason the following words supply me, eis ton kosmon eiselthe, entered into the world. But that by the world all humans are understood, since you and almost all interpreters confess it, there is no need to prove. I reason therefore thus: The sin which entered through Adam into all humans is not Adam's actual sin, but hereditary corruption. But the Apostle speaks of the sin which entered through Adam into all humans. Therefore he speaks not of Adam's actual sin, but of hereditary corruption.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: minor clear / major agreed; tip before GAR Cap. VII
english: The Minor is clear. How the Major could be denied I do not see. For it is agreed and convenes between us that through Adam hereditary corruption which is truly sin entered into all humans: which being posited, what is there why we should not take the Apostle's words of it?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR Cap. VII § IX — actual by reatus, corruption by inhesion
english: GAR. Adam's actual sin passes into all humans no less than corruption. Namely corruption by inhesion, Adam's sin by reatus and imputation.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — actual not intra nos; imputation in God
english: PLAC. Does it then pass into all humans no less, or as the Apostle speaks, enter, than corruption? Is Adam's actual sin therefore inside us, no less than corruption? Or can it be inside us, and yet not be in us, not inhere? That imputation is outside us, in God, and was made long before we were: Adam's actual sin also ceased to be some thousands of years before we began to be. How then can it be said to have entered into us, and indeed by that imputation?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — habitual agreed; actual denied; two entry-modes
english: Next it is agreed between us that habitual sin entered through one man into all humans, and experience itself confirms it; but it is not agreed that actual sin entered through one man into all humans; for this we flatly deny, and it cannot be proved. Our interpretation therefore cannot be denied, since it is in confession. Those who oppose us must therefore prove their interpretation, before it can or ought to be admitted. Finally since those two modes of entering, of which one is feigned, the other is certain and confessed, are wholly diverse, and one with respect to the other is either nothing or figurative, how can things so diverse be signified by one verb of entering used once?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — justification scope prefers Adam's actual
english: GAR. Since the Apostle here treats the cause of justification, not of sanctification, it is no wonder if from his primary intention he wished here rather to look at Adam's actual sin than at that inhering corruption, since the sin committed by Adam, and the reatus following from it, answers to the righteousness of Christ, and to our justification through it: but internal corruption answers not properly to that righteousness of Christ, but rather to the holiness inhering in us through the Holy Spirit. Which corruption, although here also because of that connection we have named it can be comprehended, yet does not directly regard the Apostolic aim, as in what follows Paul will treat of it openly.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — corruption truly sin; reatus even of infants
english: PLAC. What? Is corruption not truly sin? Does reatus not follow from it? Does it not make all and each human, not even little ones excepted still hiding in their mothers' womb, guilty of eternal death before God? Must we not first of all be justified from it? It is strange that those who accuse us of innovated doctrine depart so openly from the doctrine received by all Protestants.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — singular act ≠ introire/imputari; tip before GAR Resp. 1
english: Next it is plain that Adam's actual sin, since it was a singular action, and, as you yourself speak, personal, which as soon as it was passed away, could not have entered into all humans. Nor can you reply that that singular action and one in number, committed so long before we were born, entered into all humans by imputation: for who ever heard by report that this phrase, to enter into someone, signifies to be imputed to someone? Do not, I ask, to defend your opinion do violence to the word of God. That action of Adam was never inside us, but neither was its imputation, which if any existed would be God's action remaining inside God, not inside us. If you shall say that that action of Adam by which his actual sin was, is said to have entered into us, not indeed by reason of itself, but by reason of the penalty which it earned for us, namely of hereditary corruption, first again you abuse the verb of entering: for it is one thing for the penalty of sin, another for sin, to enter into someone. Our sins were imputed to Christ our surety, yet no one will say that through us sins entered into Christ, although he took their penalty upon himself.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR Cap. VIII Resp. 1 — innate corruption cannot 'enter'
english: GAR. Resp. 1. By the same subtlety it can be shown that by that sin is not to be understood (which yet those who use these reasons want) the hereditary corruption inhering in each of us from origin. For that corruption cannot be said to enter into us: since it is innate and inborn, and most deeply fixed from the beginning in our nature: but that is said to enter somewhere, which has been brought there from outside, or comes from elsewhere, and before was not there. Certainly none of us was earlier than he was corrupt.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — not the same subtlety; not local motion
english: PLAC. It would indeed be the same subtlety, if my argument could be accommodated equally to corruption and to actual sin: but now since this subtlety of the learned man is situated in an argument very diverse from mine, I cannot understand why it is called the same subtlety, or what it harms in my arguments? Although it has no force. For who does not see that by that entry of sin is not to be understood an entry situated in local motion which is proper to bodies and substances?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — entered by propagation; leprosy analogy; Non entis
english: Who also, unless he is a Pelagian, does not understand that sin entered into humans by natural propagation as soon as we are begotten, and therefore was not brought from outside into those already born? namely it is said to have entered into us, because it truly is inside us, and yet is not from creation, or from human nature itself, but from elsewhere, from the serpent's temptation and the first man's actual sin. And so truly through one man that vice entered into human nature where before it was not, nor ought to be, and together with nature into us all, which cannot be said of actual sin. What therefore is innate, if it is not from nature, nothing can prohibit that it be said to have entered through parents into children. So it can be said that through a parent leprosy or gout entered into children, although leprosy is in the children from birth. Not indeed earlier in time, but earlier yet by nature we were than we were corrupt. For corruption of nature cannot but be later than nature itself. But if we were not earlier than we were corrupt, and corruption follows, Of a non-being there are no accidents.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR 2 — Amyraut: Christ's justice said to enter
english: GAR. 2. It is not more absurd if it is said that sin, or Adam's singular action, entered, than if it is said that Christ's righteousness entered. But so speaks the distinguished Amyraut in a paraphrase of this verse: through one man who is Jesus Christ, true righteousness was introduced into the world, which is said of imputed righteousness no less than of inhering. To those whom it does not displease if imputed righteousness is said to be introduced or to enter, why should it not please, if imputed sin also is said to enter?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Amyraut means remission, not imputed-only entry
english: PLAC. Did the distinguished Amyraut say that the righteousness which inhered in Christ entered through him alone into humans? Certainly not: And yet that ought to have been said by him, so that by his locution the learned man's exposition could be defended. Namely by the name of righteousness which through one man was introduced into the world, either I am badly mistaken, or with Calvin he understood the remission of sins, and wished it introduced not into all humans, or into all believers by imputation alone, but obtained by Christ and given by the Father and offered to all by the preaching of the Gospel and accepted by faith by believers, in whom it remains constant: which cannot similarly be said of Adam's actual sin.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR 3 — 'enter' as begin-to-be; tip before PLAC reply
english: GAR. 3. What is often said to be introduced is that which then at last begins to be, as among the Greeks eis to dikasterion eiselthein, to enter into judgment, is to begin a suit. And Christ is said to have entered, and to have been introduced into the world, when in the world he began to be according to his humanity. Acts 1. 21. Heb. 1. 6. Therefore when sin first began to be in the human race, which was through the first parents' disobedience, it is rightly said to have entered into the world.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — drowning grasp; Greek 'enter judgment' ≠ begin-to-be
english: PLAC. After the manner of those who are drowning, the learned man seizes whatever meets him: but in vain. For grant that the phrase eis to dikasterion eiselthein among the Greeks signifies to begin a suit, does it follow that the same verb constructed with any other noun is used for 'to begin'? Will, for example, eiselthein eis ton oikon, or eis ten polin, be to begin a house or a city, or so to begin to be in a house or city, that you were not there before?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Acts 1:21 Hebraism of going in/out, not birth
english: The place Acts 1. 21. is wrongly praised: for to go in and to go out is a Hebraism, signifying neither birth nor death, but conversation, and the functions of either public or private offices. See Beza's Annot. on that place.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Heb 1:6 second advent; Bellarmine/Chamierus
english: The other place also, Heb. 1. 6., refutes the learned man: for it is not to be understood of Christ's nativity, but of his second most glorious advent, as is plain from the Apostle's words, and from the whole of Ps. 97. from which they are taken. Moreover Bellarmine refuted this reply of the learned man with many reasons in book 4. de amiss. Grat. chapter 3. and after him Chamier, but more briefly, in book 1. de hom. corrupt. chapter 5. section 9.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — Isa 53:6; sins 'came' on Christ → Adam's on us
english: Why then may I not say that our sins eiselthein into Christ, when Scripture says they came into Christ? The Lord made the iniquities of us all to come, or to fall upon him. Isaiah 53. 6. And likewise, that Adam's sin elthein upon us, came upon us, because we sustain its reatus, that is, because it has been imputed to us? And so although to enter simply put is not the same as to impute, yet for sin to enter, or to come upon someone, if the matter or place where the phrase is held so requires, can be the same as for that sin to be imputed to him.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Pighius defense; pious ear refuses sins entered Christ
english: PLAC. Pighius's exposition could not have been defended more carefully than it is by the learned man in this place: for he moves no stone that he may wrest from the orthodox the argument which they are accustomed to draw against Pelagius and Pighius from the Apostle's words, through one man sin entered into the world. But he labors in vain. Truth cannot be stormed. What is it, why the learned man demands to be granted to himself, that the compound eiselthein differs in signification not at all from the simple elthein? Or who will bear one saying that our sins entered into Christ, or that through us sin entered into Christ? Does not a pious conscience flee such a locution?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Isa verb/penalty; tip before imputatum-est reductio
english: The place Isaiah 53. 6. is not to the point, both because it is not the same verb: for hiphgia is not 'he made to enter' or 'to go in,' but 'he made to meet,' or 'to fall upon'; and because iniquity in that place signifies not the sin itself, but the penalty of sin. For it met Christ, falls upon him, rushes upon him, and, if you will, entered into him—not sin, but only the penalty of sin. But here sin is distinguished from the penalty of sin: for there follows, and through sin death. And so it cannot be proved that it can be the same, for sin to enter into someone, and for sin to be imputed to someone. But if sin, insofar as it is distinguished from penalty, entered into Christ, what is there why Christ could not have been called a sinner? If this is absurd, that also must be confessed to be absurd.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — imputatum-est substitution; Apostolic speech ruined
english: But, that every obstinacy may be stormed, in place of introiit put imputatum est, see how finely the Apostle's speech will proceed: through one man sin was imputed to the world, and through sin death. Was death imputed? Was it imputed through sin? Was sin imputed through Adam? Do they not make the Apostle ridiculous, as far as in them lies, who so dispute against me?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR 5 — singular act enters by reatus, not substance
english: GAR. 5. And so although a singular action, by reason of its substance, cannot be said to enter into another, yet by reason of reatus it is rightly said to enter, insofar as because of that action another is held guilty, and so lies under penalties.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — action ≠ reatus; relation cannot transfer the act
english: PLAC. But 1. action is one thing, reatus another. That is an action, this a relation, that passes, this remains. Is it then, if reatus is rightly said to enter, rightly also said that the action enters? Can whatever is said of reatus also be said of the action? Is action a relation? Does it remain after the action has passed? Does it follow the action? 2. It is one thing to be held guilty because of an action, another for the reatus of the action to enter into someone: that signifies only an external denomination, this imports something more. Nay the reatus itself, since it is a relation, cannot be said to enter, except either by reason of the foundation, that is, of sin whether it be action or habit, or of the term, that is, of penalty, so far is it from it that by reason of reatus the action can be said to enter into another.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR 6 — imputation as God's action entering by effects
english: GAR. 6. Finally the imputation of sin is indeed that action of God, proceeding from God as judge, but tending into humans, as into a term, and in that respect entering or coming into a human, because of the effects which it produces in him, that is, because of the penalties with which it afflicts him. So curse is an action of God Gen. XII. 3. Malachi 2. 2. And yet it is said to enter into some humans Psalm 109. 18. The curse shall enter, like water, within him, and like oil into his bones. But that the imputation of sin is an action of God remaining inside God theologians hardly grant, who are accustomed to distinguish God's actions into immanent and transeunt; they call immanent those which terminate in God himself, as intellection, and volition, by which he understands and loves himself: transeunt, those which terminate in creatures, such as the actions of divine providence. But these I leave to be disputed by others.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Ps 109 curse is effect; imputation would be through God
english: PLAC. Who ever denied that God's actions are some immanent, some transeunt; those in God, these in creatures?
