And who does not know that into this latter kind must be placed the curse which is an action of God? Although by the curse in Psalm 109. 18. is not signified the action, but rather the effect of an angry God, namely misery, misfortune, the evil of penalty. The Prophet wants a man of this kind to be clothed and penetrated on every side with all bodily and spiritual evils. And so it preceded, he wished that the curse would befall him, and there follows, Let this be the reward of those opposing me, etc. But what does this do for the matter we are treating? It is asked in what sense the Apostle said that through one man sin entered into the world, that is, into humans? You say that by sin Adam's action must be understood. I ask, how could Adam's action, which long before any other humans were, had been past and had ceased to be, be said to have entered into all humans? You say it entered by imputation. I reply, that imputation is not the action of that one man, but of God alone. Not therefore through one man, but through God, did sin enter into all humans: than which nothing more absurd can be said.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — actual never inside us; tip before three senses
english: I reply also, that by that imputation it does not come about that the actual sin, or that past action of Adam, ever was inside us, or can be. I reply finally that imputation is either an action of the mind or of the divine judgment reckoning us to be guilty of that Adamic action, or a declaration of that divine judgment by a sentence passed in external speech, or the infliction of penalty.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — first sense: immanent act in God's mind
english: If you choose the first, it is an immanent action of God: for it is not elsewhere, nor can it be, than in God, in God's mind. Some theologians indeed call the actions of the divine mind and will actions toward the outside, because they have creatures for their object: but they do not therefore make them less immanent, as the learned man does in this place, rather inconsiderately.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — second sense: where/when is the declaration?
english: If the second, where and when was that declaration made, and is it outside us, or inside us? The learned man does not say.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — third sense: penalty enters, not sin; two entries
english: If the third, the Apostle conflicts, who in this place distinguishes sin from the penalty of sin which he calls death. By the infliction of penalty, that is, of death, death or penalty indeed enters, but sin does not enter. One thing in the Apostle's words is the entry of sin, another the entry of death; that is the cause of this.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — 'entered' fits hereditary properly, actual only remotely
english: Next, if Adam's actual sin did not enter into the world except by reason of hereditary corruption, it must be confessed that this attribute of having entered into the world, or into humans, agrees of itself and properly and nearest with hereditary corruption, only remotely, and by reason of that corruption, with Adam's actual sin. If therefore that corruption is truly and properly sin, even after baptism, as ours hold against the Papists, is it not manifest that the sin which entered into the world is rather its description than that of Adam's actual sin?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — death entered really; many deaths, not Adam's alone
english: To this is added that the Apostle says that through this sin death entered into the world. Entry into the world is a common attribute of sin and of death. Both entered into the world, but sin of itself, death through sin. But death entered in very deed, not by imputation, and the death which entered into the world is not the death of one Adam, but as manyfold as there are humans. Since therefore it is agreed there is a sin, namely hereditary corruption, which entered into the world in exactly the same way, what is there why we should not understand that in this place rather than that which corresponds to death neither by entry into the world, nor by number?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — if actual, Apostle omitted inhering or hid it under death
english: Finally if by the sin which entered into the world Adam's actual sin is understood, it is necessary that the Apostle either wholly omitted inhering corruption, or comprehended it under the name of death. Both of these are false; Therefore that also.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — if omit hereditary: not from Adam–Christ collation
english: For if you shall say that he passed over hereditary corruption, two things will follow: One, that it cannot be gathered from this whole collation which the Apostle instituted between the first and the second Adam. For in the following verses he does not teach that other evils flowed from Adam into the human race than those which he named in this v. 12. But that will greatly help Pighius's cause.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — scarce other locus ties corruption from Adam to all
english: And although there are other places in the sacred letters from which it can be made out that we are born corrupt with sin, yet there is almost no other which teaches that that corruption, proceeding from Adam himself, invaded into all humans. That scarcity matters here.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — omit → no corruption or Paul missed his scope; Pelagians win
english: The other, either that that corruption is nothing, or that the Apostle wandered from his aim. If the former, the Pelagians have won, and free choice is still intact. The latter is plain.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Paul's scope: evils from first Adam, goods from second
english: For the Apostle's aim is to teach what evils from the first Adam, what goods by contrast from the second Adam, flowed into the human race, so that we may understand it is not wonderful, when one man was so powerful to destroy us, that one man, Jesus Christ, can save us. And so he accurately compares the goods proceeded from this one into us with the evils proceeded from that one. Who therefore would believe that he wished to pass over in silence that evil which it is agreed both is derived from Adam into us, and is the cause of all our sins?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — if death-name = hereditary: leaves interpreters; helps Pelagians
english: But if you shall say that the Apostle comprehended that hereditary corruption, which is sin, under the name of death, first you will depart from the consent of all interpreters (whom I have seen). Next you will help the cause of the Pelagians against Augustine, who take the name of death of the death of the soul.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — absolute 'death' ≠ corruption; tip before all-are-sinners proof
english: Then you will bring in the Apostle against his custom, with the name of death set absolutely, and without any addition, signifying corruption of that kind, and one and the same name set once, to be understood once, taking it at once properly and figuratively. Besides, who would believe that death, when it is distinguished from sin, as is done in this place, signifies sin?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — all sinners because all die; not from latent corruption
english: Add that the Apostle proves in this place that all humans are sinners, that sin is in the world, that is in humans, by this argument, that all die. Do you think he proves that sin is in humans, because there is sin in humans, namely hereditary corruption? Does he draw the argument from a latent moral corruption, which itself was to be proved, when it was at hand from the open and known death of all?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — condemnation & death correlatives; condemned to death not sin
english: Certainly condemnation and death are correlatives with the Apostle in this chapter. We are condemned to death, not to sin. Death is not the cause of condemnation, but the effect. On the contrary sin (but hereditary corruption is sin, as I have already often said) is the cause of condemnation, not the effect.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — v.21 reign unto death; law made sin abound = concupiscence
english: Finally, that I may not be too prolix, when the Apostle says in verse 21. that sin reigned unto death, is it likely that death is taken in another way than in the Apostle's preceding dispute, of which that verse is the conclusion? But surely in that verse it cannot signify that which is truly sin. For that preceded in verse 20. the law moreover entered, that sin might abound. But where sin abounded, there grace superabounded. For that reign of sin, this overflow of sin, embraces all that in a human which is truly sin, and it is clear from Rom. VI. and VII. that that sin which overflowed and reigned through the law is concupiscence, or hereditary corruption.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — status: actual cut from hereditary; imputation precedes
english: You will perhaps think you can turn aside the edge of these arguments by saying that by sin, ten hamartian, both are understood, both Adam's actual sin, and the original vice born from it; but that is not allowed you by the status of the question which is treated between us. For it is instituted concerning Adam's actual sin cut off from hereditary vice. For you will have the first actual sin to have been imputed to Adam and to us, and because imputed, this penalty to have been inflicted on Adam and on us, namely original vice or corruption. And so according to your opinion that corruption does not cohere with Adam's actual sin except by the intervention of divine imputation. Wherefore imputation in the order of nature precedes corruption. Therefore the imputation of Adam's actual sin cut off from hereditary corruption must be proved by you, not however of it joined and confused with that.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — 'entered the world' joins hereditary vice, not bare actual
english: Which suggests other arguments to me, but, for the sake of avoiding too much prolixity in this place, to be conferred to another place. Add that I have already proved that actual sin did not enter into the world, that is, into humans: whence it follows that this attribute entered into the world joins sin to itself, not insofar as it signifies actual sin, but insofar as it signifies the vice arisen from it in my opinion immediately, but in yours by the mediation of God's imputation. So I think I have confirmed my argument enough.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — death = threatened penalty; tip before ἐφ' ᾧ / ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες
english: You see the Apostle's first words, which are the basis of those that follow; but of them at least I detect no vestige in your treatise. What if I from there elicit something adverse to your opinion. Will you grant me that by death in this place is to be understood that death which the law had threatened to Adam, namely the penalty, and the wages of sin? I do not see by what right you can deny that, especially since you hold that that law regards the whole human race, and that Adam, as God had threatened, died. You will at least grant that death in this place signifies the penalty of the sin which entered into the world.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — if 'death' = all penalties, hereditary vice still not among them
english: But you will have that sin to be Adam's actual sin, and its penalty to be not only the death of the body and eternal death, but chiefly the spiritual death of the soul, placed in the privation of original righteousness, and in hereditary corruption: from which it follows that that corruption is contained under the name of death in this place. And yet I have already proved that it is not contained. But if the Apostle by the name of death signified whatever of penalty was derived through Adam into his posterity, and yet did not under that name embrace hereditary corruption or vice, as I have already proved, you see what follows, namely that that hereditary vice is not in the number of the penalties which Adam brought upon the world, and therefore that his actual sin was not imputed to the world unto that penalty, namely hereditary vice.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον; linger then flee to ἥμαρτον; Calvin French
english: Let us come to the following words, eph' hoi pantes hemarton. Here, forsooth, you think you have found a great defense of your cause. You linger a little on the words eph' hoi, presently, leaving them, you betake yourself to the word hemarton. Namely you were unwilling wholly to reject the version which our Churches use, although you openly enough show that it does not please you. And so, you say, let our French version stand and remain, which is John Calvin's, because, or when, all have sinned. Yet against it you cast some things in this chapter and in chapter ix., which, when I shall have come to that chapter, God helping, I will call back to examination.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — ἐφ' ᾧ = eo quod not in quo; first half of verse already taken
english: And although it almost nothing concerns me how eph' hoi is rendered, because, or in which, yet I will show that it is to be turned because, and I will defend the version which our Churches approve. Meanwhile you will have these words explained because or in which all have sinned, from the first part of the verse. But I have already wrested that first part from you. If therefore all are said to have sinned by that sin which entered into the world,

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — peccaverunt with Calvin = innate vice, not Adam's bare actual
english: And that sin you have not proved to be Adam's actual sin, but I have proved it to be an inhering vice: what remains, except that we interpret that they sinned with Calvin of the vice innate and implanted in each of us? So to sin, he says, is to be corrupt and vitiated. In French: Now this sin, of which he speaks here, signifies nothing else but that we are all corrupted: for that natural depravity which we bring from our mother's womb, although it does not so soon put forth its fruits, is yet sin before the Lord, and deserves his vengeance. And a little after, we have therefore all sinned, because we are all imbued with natural corruption: and therefore iniquitous and perverse.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — active ἥμαρτον ≠ your actual-by-imputation; Pelagius risk
english: Yet you deny that this satisfies you: for, you say, the Apostle does not say since sin is in all (nay, he says this in the following verse) but, since all have sinned, eph' hoi pantes hemarton, and he uses an active verb, that he may signify actual sin, of which all are partakers. But in original sin we have not sinned by act, except insofar as we sinned in Adam: for when he sinned he sinned for all his posterity, and all men who were born of him sinned in him, because in him all were. The force of proving, if there is any, in those words of yours, consists in this, that the word hemarton, they sinned, being active, signifies actual sin. The rest are petitions of what was in the beginning. And yet that active verb, if it signifies actual sin, surely signifies actual sin committed by him himself who sinned. Bring forward, if you can, a contrary example. See therefore lest this observation of yours favor Pelagius.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — if peccaverunt = actual then not original; tip before GAR Resp.1
english: Next it does not escape you that all theologians distinguish actual sin from original. If therefore this word they sinned signifies actual sin, then it does not signify original, which you yourself in this place distinguish from the actual. Therefore the Apostle does not speak of original sin in this place. So, as much as in you lies, you wrest from us the weapons with which from this place we overthrow Pelagius, Pighius, and Socinus. But it pleases you to attack by another way: for although now indeed my part is to answer, yours to argue, yet I cannot restrain myself from scattering everywhere the arguments with which my cause abounds. Tell me therefore, I pray, how you understand all men to have sinned by Adam's actual sin? You inculcate everywhere that that actual sin cannot be ours except by imputation. If it is not ours except by imputation, then surely we have not sinned by it except by imputation. What then will that be, all have sinned? Actual sin has been imputed to all? And yet it is one thing for someone to sin, another for sin to be imputed to someone.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR Resp.1 — aliud peccare / in alio peccavisse; latter = imputation
english: GAR. I answer 1. It is one thing if you say simply that someone sins, another if you say that someone has sinned in another. For the former, surely by force of the word, does not signify imputation of sin, but this latter designates imputation. For how can those who existed many ages afterward be said to have already before sinned in another, except because he exercised their act, and he of the posterity is so reputed, as if they themselves had committed it?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — posterity 'sinned in another' as Christ-satisfaction analogy
english: So for someone to satisfy, and for satisfaction to be imputed to someone, are surely far diverse. And yet when the theologians teach that we have satisfied in Christ, they mean nothing else than that Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us. Or that Christ exhibited that satisfaction which, because of the union which we have with him as our spiritual and mystical head, is imputed to us, so that before God we are held as if we ourselves had satisfied through ourselves.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Scripture never says we sinned in Adam; 'in Adam' ≠ imputation
english: PLAC. First, Scripture does not say that we sinned in Adam. Next, I do not see why that manner of speaking should signify imputation by which another's sin, namely Adam's, becomes or exists as ours. For we are said to die in Adam, and yet Adam's death is not imputed to us.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — die/created/ejected in Adam without those acts imputed
english: We can be said to have been created in Adam, to have been created just and blessed, to have been cast out of paradise, and so on, and yet neither his creation, nor original righteousness, nor casting out of paradise is imputed to us. Therefore we could be said to have sinned in him, in the way we can be said to have been in him, because he communicated to us both his nature and his sin by natural propagation.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Christ surety ≠ Adam; we were not bound to sin as to satisfy
english: As for Christ's satisfaction, when we are said to have satisfied in Christ, nothing else seems to me to be understood, except that Christ in our place satisfied for us: did Adam therefore likewise in our place sin for us? Each of us was bound to satisfy for himself. That was impossible for us. Christ, who was not bound, constituted himself our surety, and satisfied for us. Can the same be said of us and of Adam? Were we bound to sin? Did Adam constitute himself our surety, that he might sin for us?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — union/faith before imputation of Christ's satisfaction; tip before GAR 2
english: I ask also, when did we satisfy in Christ? I think when he suffered. Was Christ's satisfaction therefore then imputed to us? Then therefore we were justified, not yet existing, not yet believing. We are therefore not justified by faith, seeing that our justification so far preceded both our existence and our faith. Add that we do not have union with Christ as our spiritual and mystical head except by faith; it follows therefore that the imputation of Christ's satisfaction, or our justification, follows our faith. What reason is there why we should not similarly say that we do not have union with Adam as head of sinners except by the hereditary vice by which he communicated his sin with us? And so the imputation of Adam's sin is later than that vice.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR 2 — peccandi verbum sometimes = consequent reatus (antecedent for consequent)
english: GAR. 2. Nor is it unknown in Scripture that the word of sinning sometimes signifies the guilt consequent from sin, according to that manner of speaking by which the antecedent is put for the consequent.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — Judah Gen 43 & Bathsheba: 'I will sin' = be held guilty
english: As when Judah, about to take Benjamin with him into Egypt, addresses his father Jacob thus, Genesis XLIII. I pledge for him; of my hand require him: If I do not bring him back to you, and set him before you, I shall altogether have sinned against you all my days, that is, I shall be guilty to you, and shall be held by you for a criminal: So Bathsheba to David, 1 Kings I. 21. when the lord king sleeps with his fathers, I and my son Solomon shall be sinners; that is, it shall be dealt with us as with the guilty and the accused, as the interpreters explain.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — so 'sin in Adam' may = be held guilty as if we ourselves sinned
english: What then will be new in this, if we teach that the same metalepsis familiar to the Hebrews is used here, so that we are said to sin in Adam, that is, to be held as guilty, no less than if, Adam sinning, we ourselves had sinned?. Mark that well.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Pighian reply; Martyr: many made sinners = vice in those born of Adam
english: PLAC. Since this reply is Pighian, and was formerly objected to our men, let Martyr refute it while I am silent, Commentary on Romans 5. 9. and Common Places, Class 2. chapter 1. section 8. Finally, he says, we have from Paul, that by the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners; which indicates that in those who are born of Adam there is a vice because of which they can be called sinners. But Pighius thinks he can elude this, because sinners are sometimes so called because of guilt although the act of sinning has passed and no longer exists.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — sinner-name needs vice in self or prior act; Paul teaches true sin propagated
english: Although this is so, yet he can never show from the Scriptures that anyone is called a sinner unless he either has vice in himself, or has certainly committed it before: unless he would say that God makes men guilty without some sin of their own. I confess therefore that those who are punished or oppressed by calamity are called sinners, but not before God, unless they themselves have either committed sin, or have it in themselves: And truly it is manifest that the Apostle is at this in this place, that he may teach that sin has truly been propagated into all humans, not however something which is not sin, but only a consequent of sin.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — if peccatum figurative here, orthodox arms vs Pelagius fail; tip before GAR Resp.3
english: If the name of sin is not taken properly in this place, but figuratively, by that figure by which the antecedent is put for the consequent, how do the Orthodox argue from this place against Pelagius and Pighius? And, if it is taken properly, how is it at the same time taken figuratively?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — men may impute falsely; God imputes because one sinned
english: Men, whether ignorant or unjust, sometimes impute to other men sins who have not sinned; and to those who have sinned God sometimes does not impute sins: And, if to anyone God imputes sin, he imputes because he has sinned; he does not by imputing make him to have sinned. In the order of nature it is first sinned, before sin is imputed.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR Resp.3 — God imputes to none unless he sinned in self or in another (Saul)
english: GAR. Answer 3. God imputes sin to no one unless he has sinned either in himself, or in another, that is, unless either he has committed sin in himself, or another with whom he is closely joined; as he imputed Saul's sin to his sons, not because they themselves had committed it, but because their father had committed it. And likewise God testifies in the law that he visits the sins of the fathers upon the children.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — imputing does not make one to have sinned; judicial declaration of reus
english: God, by imputing sin to someone, does not make him to have sinned, but supposes him to have sinned, whether in himself or in another. For the imputation of sin is a judicial act of God, by which he declares someone to be guilty and worthy of penalty on account of sin, as was said from the beginning.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — sin precedes imputation; need conjunction with sinner (Amyraut)
english: It is sinned first by someone, before sin is imputed; but it is not necessary that by that very one to whom sin is imputed, sin should first have been by act; but it is necessary that he have some conjunction with him who sinned, and whose sin is imputed to him, as the learned Amyraut taught before.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — three replies same sound; conjunction as sinner ≠ as origin alone
english: PLAC. Those three replies of the learned man seem to me to sound the same; I will therefore refute them all together. First the conjunction with the sinner must be distinguished: for one is conjunction with the sinner insofar as he is a sinner, another with the sinner insofar as he is the man from whom we draw our origin. He cannot be free from sin who is joined with the sinner insofar as he is a sinner: for he is a partaker of the same sin, whether by consent, or by propagation, or by imitation, and so on.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — origin-only link would impute all parent sins; Saul's house; tip before contradiction
english: But conjunction with another, insofar as he is the man from whom we draw origin, alone does not suffice for a sin committed by another to be imputed: otherwise all Adam's sins, and all our parents' sins, could rightly be imputed to us, which, I think, no one would say: yet no other conjunction between us and Adam could have existed before the hereditary corruption communicated by him. Nor does the example of Saul help the learned man: For his sons, when they were sinners in themselves and worthy on account of their own sins of those penalties which they suffered, were then also partakers of that paternal sin, as is clear from the words of God himself, 2 Samuel 21. 1. For Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites. Therefore not Saul alone was bloody, but his house or family.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — learned man inconsistent: in alio peccare = imputation, then prior to it
english: Next the learned man does not seem to himself to stand consistent enough. For he had said in the preceding paragraph that for someone to sin in another designates imputation by force of the word, and that to sin in another and for another's sin to be imputed are the same. Now he will have them to be diverse; and that to sin in another is prior to another's sin being imputed; and that this as the later, that as the prior and cause.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — if Adam's sin ours only by imputation, circular 'we sinned in Adam'
english: Next he inculcates everywhere that Adam's sin is not ours except by imputation: whence it follows that we did not sin in Adam except by imputation. And yet now he will have Adam's sin imputed to us, because we sinned in Adam. But how did we sin in Adam, if Adam's sin was not ours? Therefore as we first sinned in Adam before his sin was imputed to us, so Adam's sin was first ours before it was imputed to us. How then does he inculcate everywhere that it is not ours except by imputation?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Deus imputando non facit peccatores; entry not by imputation
english: Finally God, he says, by imputing sin to someone does not make him to have sinned. Therefore God by imputing does not make Adam's posterity to be sinners. For he is not a sinner who has not sinned. How then does the learned man say that by Adam's actual sin, because of imputation, we are constituted sinners by Adam's disobedience by imputation? In one word, if we are sinners before God imputes Adam's sin to us, Adam's sin did not enter into the world by imputation, but imputation follows that entry: which was what I had to prove.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — being in Adam before peccare; not by imputation of his being
english: Next you will have all to have sinned in Adam. But you will grant that they were in Adam in the way they sinned in Adam: for it is prior to be than to act or to sin. Were we therefore in Adam by an imputation of his being? You will deny it far from doubt: why then will you have us to have sinned in him by an imputation of his sinning?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — if peccare ≠ imputari, explain other mode you always deny
english: You will perhaps say that that to sin does not signify sin to be imputed. From this I will infer, therefore all sinned by actual sin, not because it is imputed to them, but in another way, which I desire to be explained to me by you, who so often deny that Adam's actual sin is ours in any other way than by imputation.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — when in paradise we 'properly' sinned → infant was then; tip before GAR jest charge
english: But besides I ask. When did we sin in Adam by his actual sin? when he sinned it, or at another time? without doubt when he committed it in paradise: you can assign no other time. Hear what follows from that. Those who have so sinned that they have merited for themselves the just condemnation of eternal death, those have truly and properly sinned. But those who have truly and properly sinned, those then when they sinned were truly and properly. Therefore he who today begins to be and is born an infant, he truly and properly speaking already then was, when Adam was in paradise, some thousands of years before: inasmuch as he then truly and properly sinned. And so what Christ said of himself, John 8. 58. Before Abraham was born I am, there will be none of us who cannot say the same of himself.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — jest charge: rather lose a hundred jokes than abuse Scripture
english: GAR. Answer 1. From the words of our Lord and God, Hebrew commas—whether you expose others to mockery in jest or in earnest—let others' judgment be. I would rather lose a hundred jokes for myself than be willing to abuse even a little word of sacred Scripture.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — serio: John 8:58 reductio shows immediate imputation absurd
english: PLAC. Have I here woven jokes or commas? Nay, in earnest, most of all, I say, I have argued in earnest, and have uncovered the absurdity of immediate imputation. For what jest is there in this argument? From which opinion it follows that each one of us can say of himself what Christ said of himself, Before Abraham was, I am—that is false and absurd. But that follows from the opinion by which we are said to have truly and properly sinned, and so to have been then when Adam was still in the earthly paradise. Therefore that opinion is false and absurd. When I so argue, do I seem to you, Reader, to jest, and to abuse Scripture for a joke? I do not think so. Yet the words I have used contain nothing else than this argument.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — Christ-words for a creature? Calvin & Augustine forbid
english: GAR. And there can be some reason why someone should apply to an infant or to any man whatever those words by which, Calvin testifying, Christ exempts himself from the common crowd of men, and claims for himself alone the divine power, whose sense from the beginning of the world has been diffused through all ages. Do you think holy Augustine would have suffered this place to be accommodated to a creature, whether in jest or in earnest—he who, when he had diligently meditated those words, exclaims, Acknowledge the Creator, discern the creature?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — I hold Calvin/Augustine; reject your opinion for that absurd consequent
english: PLAC. The learned man seems to dispute for me, against himself. For I think the same with Calvin and Augustine, and that, I think, I have sufficiently testified in Disputation xi. book 1. for the Divine nature of our Lord Jesus Christ; and now also I testify, who for that reason reject your opinion in this place, because from it follows the greatest absurdity, namely that those words of Christ can suit any other man. If this consequent seems absurd to you, as it certainly is, and indeed as absurd as can be, why does the antecedent from which it is drawn not seem equally absurd to you?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — same subtilty vs Christ-satisfaction / Socinian counter-thrust
english: GAR. 2. But consider the vain subtilty of the reasoning in a like example. So Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us, that we are said to have satisfied in Christ. Let someone from the flock of the Socinians approach; about to take mutual arms against that doctrine, he will rise against the learned man and against the truth with subtle argumentation. When then at last do we satisfy in Christ, by his actual satisfaction? When Christ himself satisfied on the cross? Or at another time? Surely when he satisfied on the cross. But hear. Those who have satisfied so as to placate the wrath of God, those have truly and properly satisfied. Those who have truly and properly satisfied, then when they satisfied, truly and properly were. Therefore has the Christian who now lives truly been, when Christ hung on the cross? What seems? Is it not a strongly twisted dart? Let him who taught to knot it loose the knot. For he will not refute the Socinian so as not also by the same reason to traduce his own subtilty.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — satisfaction imputed after faith, not before existence; tip before 'alius pro nobis'
english: PLAC. This example is not like, nor does it in any way overturn my reasoning. Christ's satisfaction is indeed imputed to us believing, but that imputation follows our faith, does not precede it, still less so as to precede our existence. For we are justified by faith, not before faith. When therefore we are said to have satisfied in Christ, as the phrase does not stand in Scripture, so it ought to be taken conveniently, and cannot be understood properly. The sense ought to be no other than this, Christ satisfied for us.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — can we say of sin 'another sinned for us / in our place'?
english: We have not satisfied, but another, namely Christ, has satisfied for us. Can the same be said of sin: We have not sinned, but another has sinned for us, or in our place?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — 'when do we satisfy?' hints dual satisfaction; only one from Christ
english: Next the question, When then at last do we satisfy in Christ by his actual satisfaction? is not far from ridiculous: for it hints a double satisfaction, actual and habitual; whereas yet not, as there is one actual sin committed by Adam, another habitual propagated into us and inhering in us, so is there any satisfaction besides that which was performed by Christ in our place.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — split double question: when Christ satisfied vs when imputed
english: Besides, the proposition when we satisfy in Christ, since it is not proper, needs exposition, and is to be recalled to the proper: otherwise the fallacy of many questions is committed: for it contains these two questions: 1. When did Christ satisfy? 2. When is Christ's satisfaction imputed to us? To that I answer, when he suffered on the cross; to this, when we believe in him.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — same split for Adam: act in paradise vs imputation; propagation suffices
english: But if you similarly resolve the question, When did we sin in Adam? into these two, When did Adam sin? and, When is his sin imputed to us? the answer to the first will be easy, when he ate the forbidden fruit in paradise; to the second, not to say that imputation is supposed, whereas yet, that we may be said to have sinned in Adam, imputation is not necessary, propagation of sin suffices, I answer, when we were begotten of Adam vitiated and corrupted.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — we 'sinned in Adam' when born corrupted; opponent cannot so answer
english: What absurdity is there in that? And yet the learned man could not so answer, inasmuch as he will have Adam's sin to have been imputed to us already from that time when Adam fell.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — many discriminations Christ-satisfaction vs Adam-sin; tip before GAR Pelagian telum
english: For the rest, how many discriminations there are between Christ's satisfaction and Adam's sin we have already observed several times, and will observe at Romans 5. 19.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — Pelagian telum: sin-in-Adam = hereditary corruption?
english: GAR. 3. But the Pelagian also will seize a dart, and will twist it against us. For where the Apostle says that we have sinned in Adam, what does the learned man understand by the word sin? Hereditary corruption, that original vice of ours, and inborn in us. And so to have sinned in Adam will be to have been corrupt and vitiated in Adam.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — when corrupted in Adam? same reductio as before
english: The Pelagian will now rise, and relying on this argumentation will ask, When were we corrupted in Adam by his sin? When he himself sinned, and by sinning corrupted himself, or at another time? Surely when he himself sinned, and by sinning corrupted himself. Many, nay all, have been warned by the sin for us, but also by the vice of that fall. Hear now. Those who were so corrupted that they were made guilty of eternal death, those were truly and properly corrupted. Those who were truly and properly corrupted, those then when they were corrupted truly and properly were. Therefore has the infant who is now born truly been, when Adam was sinning, and by sinning corrupting himself? So those who had made snares for others put themselves into them, and into the pit which they had prepared for others they themselves fall.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Apostle never said we sinned in Adam; sense = derived corruption
english: PLAC. These snares are none, nor do I easily get free. For first the Apostle has not said that we have sinned in Adam, and even if he had said it, what sense the proposition that we are corrupt and vitiated in Adam can have must be considered. The sense is that we are corrupted by corruption derived from Adam, or, which comes to the same, that Adam's corruption was the fountain from which our corruption sprang, or, that Adam was corrupted, and Adam's corruption was propagated into us.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Adam corrupted when he first sinned; we when born
english: If therefore I ask, When was Adam corrupted? I will answer, when he first sinned. When were we corrupted by force of the communion which we have with Adam? Answer, when we were begotten. What difficulty is there in that matter?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — corruptus in Adamo ≠ corruptus simpliciter; root before branches
english: I pass over that the learned man uses the fallacy from what is said in a certain respect to what is said simply. For it is one thing to be corrupt in a certain respect, or with this limitation in Adam, another to be corrupt simply or without such a limitation. This does not follow from that, if the reason of that time is had, when Adam was first corrupted: for the corruption of the root or fountain is signified, not of the branches or streams, because they were not yet. But it is prior to be than to be corrupt.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — fights pre-existence imputation; tip before GAR 4 (act+corruption)
english: Which he cannot answer me, because, as I have already observed, I oppose the imputation which is believed to have long been, before we began to be. And by that imputation it was brought about that we truly and properly became sinners and guilty.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR 4 — remember prior: Adam's sin = act + following corruption
english: GAR. 4. But so they argue: they ought to have been mindful of those things which they said before. If Adam's sin is taken not for the act itself precisely taken, but together with the corruption which it begot, Adam's sin is rightly said to be imputed to the posterity. For so it will be sin, both Adam's act itself and the following corruption.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — so rightly imputed; we sin in Adam by corruption and by his act
english: And so as we are rightly said to sin in Adam because of the corruption descending into us from Adam: so also we shall be said truly to sin in him, because of the act which Adam performed before.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — how that aids antecedent imputation unclear (pp. 151–153)
english: PLAC. How that was said before, and how much it favors antecedent imputation, we judge to appear sufficiently from what was said above at pages 151, 152, 153. Whither therefore this reply of the learned man pertains, and what force it has, I do not understand.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — our corruption is ours by propagation; the begetting act not ours
english: Certainly the corruption is ours, because propagated into us, it is within us; but the act which begot the corruption is not ours except insofar as the corruption is a certain participation of it, and there is consent unto it.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR 5 open — deny that meriting just condemnation = truly/properly sinned
english: GAR. 5. That is denied on which the learned man builds his whole reason, that those who have so sinned that they have merited just condemnation have truly and properly sinned. What if to sin truly and properly is to sin in one's own person, and to offend by one's own, not by another's, sin? For one's own is opposed to another's.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR tip — alienum peccatum can merit; Saul's sons; tip before PLAC on vere/proprie
english: And yet even those who sin by another's sin, that is, to whom another's sin is imputed, also merit just condemnation. For Saul's sons sinned by another's, namely the father's, sin, and yet they suffered the just condemnation of death by God's command, and so merited it, because God's judgments are just. And the sins by which the fathers actually sinned are not properly the sons' sins, because they were not personally committed by them; and yet according to the Decalogue's threat, because of them the sons incur various penalties and just condemnation. So therefore we can have sinned in Adam so as to have merited the just sentence of death, and yet we need not for that reason come to this, that we say we properly or personally sinned when Adam sinned; but only that we are so reckoned before God, as if when he himself sinned all of us had sinned.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — thought vere≠falso and proprie≠figurate; Vir doctus equates both with personaliter
english: PLAC. I used to think "truly" was opposed to "falsely," and "properly" to "improperly" or "figuratively," and I took them that way; but the learned man now teaches me that in this place both mean the same as "personally," or "in one's own person."

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — did they sin vere or falso? False sin cannot be damned by a just judge
english: I ask, then: those who have so sinned that they have earned a just and proper condemnation—have they sinned truly, or falsely? Falsely, I suppose, no one will say. For if someone is said to have so sinned that he has merited just condemnation, and yet one can prove that this is said falsely, it cannot be that he is damned by a just judge for a sin of that kind.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — proprie not figurate/metaphorice; penalty and sin answer each other
english: Again I ask whether he can be said to have sinned properly or not—that is, not figuratively or metaphorically. No one will say he sinned only metaphorically or figuratively: for since penalty and sin answer each other, a penalty truly and properly so called presupposes a sin truly and properly so called—another's, when the penalty is inflicted on someone as surety for the sinner; one's own, when it is inflicted on him as on a sinner who has earned a properly so-called penalty.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — born vere & proprie sinners; Augustine and great names deny damnation for another's sin alone
english: Nor can it be denied that we are born from Adam truly and properly sinners, and from him draw a sin truly and properly so called. Add that Augustine denies, and other theologians of great name deny, that anyone is damned for another's sin. See, if you will, the words of Martyr we cited above, p. 196, from Loci Communes, Class. 2, ch. 1, §11; and also Calvin's and Chamier's words cited above, pp. 95–98.

added_allusions.note: denies damnation for another's sin alone (as Placeus cites)

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Martyr vs Pighius; merit of true condemnation — 'by imputation'?
english: I will add these few words of Martyr from the same place, Loci §7: "We neither can nor ought to rest in this comment"—he means Pighius's comment—"for God's wrath is provoked only justly. Nor is it of such a kind that it can be kindled rashly or by chance. So there must be something evil in our nature, for the avenging of which the divine wrath is stirred." Otherwise, how would we merit a true and properly so-called condemnation, if we had no merit of that kind of condemnation of our own? "It is ours," you will say, "by imputation." So imputation, I reply, makes us merit an eternal penalty that otherwise we do not merit.

added_allusions.note: Martyr rejects his comment on wrath without inborn evil

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — does antecedent imputation fit God's equity, glory, and truth?
english: Whether that befits God's equity, I ask you, reader, to consider carefully. For since the end set before us ought to be God's glory, see, I pray, whether that is glorious to God, and whether it makes his equity and justice clearer. See also whether it befits his truth. We sinned in Adam; we merited the just sentence of death—and that without doubt neither falsely nor figuratively: yet we did not properly or personally sin when Adam sinned; we are only reckoned before God as if, when he himself sinned, we all had sinned. Is this judgment according to the truth? Glorious to God?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — evangelical-justice reply; sin's ratio unlike gifted righteousness
english: But someone will say: we are reckoned before God as if we were just. Yes—we truly are just, not by a legal righteousness but by an evangelical one; not by a righteousness of works but of faith; not by a righteousness that proceeds from us or is acquired by us, but given by God and received through faith. The case of sin is different: it is not promised, not given by God, not received by one who does not yet exist.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Augustine (none immune from Adam's vice); Saul's sons and fathers' sins in sons
english: Augustine's words do not hurt my case: for I grant that no one is immune from Adam's vice. As for the example of Saul's sons, we have already answered that they were partakers of the father's sin. The fathers' sins are visited on the sons, as I said, when they are found in the sons. They are called the fathers' because the fathers first committed them, and were authors to the sons that they should commit them—by example and authority, or by education and training, or even by law.

added_allusions.note: none immune from Adam's vice—Placeus grants

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Heb. 7 Levi-in-Abraham objection; phrase hard, not proper; defer to theses
english: You will object that here too you add the Apostle's saying that Levi was tithed in Abraham because he was still in his father's loins when Melchizedek met him. But the Apostle plainly hints that that phrase is not only not proper, but harsh, when he softens it with the preface "so to speak." Next, I answered that place in the theses, and you take my answer to refute it at the end of chapter 9 of your treatise; how well, when following your steps I reach that place, God helping, I will show—and by the same work I will uncover the Apostle's reasoning as most solid, yet altogether foreign to the imputation disputed between us.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — 1 Cor. 15 in Adam all die: each his own death; rise in Christ really, not by imputed resurrection
english: You also object a like phrase in a like matter from the same Apostle: in Adam all die. But that overturns your view. For he does not mean that all die in Adam by that very singular death by which Adam died, as if it were imputed to all, but each by his own proper death. So we are made alive, or rise, in Christ—not by imputation of Christ's resurrection, but by a real resurrection which each receives in himself.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — per hominem mors/resurrectio: one in kind, many in number—not imputed singular death
english: And when in the preceding verse the Apostle speaks thus—since by a man comes death, by a man also comes the resurrection of the dead—he does not mean one Adam's death imputed to the rest of men, nor one Christ's resurrection imputed, but death and resurrection one in kind, many in number, by which all die and rise, each his own. That is so plain it needs no proof.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — Rom 5 conclude: propagated sin; each own; die by natural communion, not in Adam's person
english: Let us conclude, then: when the same Apostle says that through one man sin entered the world, it is to be understood not as that singular actual sin which that one man committed, but as the sin born from him and spread and propagated into all men. And when it is said that all sinned in Adam (though he does not say that), it is to be understood that all sinned—not by that one singular actual sin of Adam imputed to them, but each by his own inborn and proper sin, which takes its origin from that of Adam. We die, then, in Adam—that is, by the force of the natural communion that joins us to Adam, not in Adam's own person; and we are made alive in Christ, not in the very person of Jesus Christ, but by the force of our supernatural communion with him: but of this again when we come to the Theses.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR Resp. 1 — denying death-devotion in Adam's person deserts Confession Art. 10
english: GAR. Resp. I. Those who deny that we were devoted to death in Adam's own person plainly desert the Confession of our churches, which teaches and expressly says that in Art. 10.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — I keep Art. 10; deny 'were devoted to death' in Adam's person (tense and wording)
english: PLAC. Do I desert that Confession, which I wholly embrace and tightly hold, especially that tenth article? Yet I deny that we were devoted to death in Adam's own person. First, those words "were devoted to death" are not mine: I did not use the past tense but the present, and I did not speak of devotion (addiction) but of death itself. For the Apostle's words run thus: in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive; they cannot be taken of a present devotion of that kind, as is clear from the future "will be made alive."

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — each dies/rises his own; deny-in-person = deny Adam's/Christ's death/rising imputed
english: I speak, then, of the death by which each dies, and of the resurrection by which each formally rises. And when I deny that we die in Adam's own person, I mean nothing else than that we die by Adam's own death imputed to us; when I deny that we rise in Christ's own person, nothing else than that we rise by Christ's resurrection imputed to us—as is plain from the very words that went before.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Art. 10 'spoiled in his person' does not yield Adam's death imputed; more in Cap. XII
english: Does that tenth article of the Confession teach the contrary? Why then am I set against it? But it says we were spoiled of all those goods in his (Adam's) person, and fell into all this misery and curse. Therefore we die in Adam's own person—that is, by Adam's death imputed to us. No such thing follows from those words of the Confession. Indeed not even any imputation can be drawn from them, either of those gifts or of that spoiling—as will be shown more fully in chapter XII.

added_allusions.note: spoiled of goods in Adam's person

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR 2 open — natural union with Adam is foundation of the imputation at issue
english: GAR. 2. We not only acknowledge a natural union with Adam, but also say that it is the foundation of that imputation which is under discussion.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — if imputation is antecedent/immediate, that union is not its foundation
english: PLAC. If the imputation is understood as antecedent or immediate, that union is not its foundation. But let him go on.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — each dies own death / own corruption; still 'die in Adam' may pertain to imputation
english: GAR. It is no less certain that each of us dies by his own proper death, and has an internal corruption proper to himself and personally distinct from the corruption which actual sin made in Adam. Yet we have both by the force of that conjunction which joins us to Adam as head of the race. Still those facts do not keep the Apostle's words from being said to pertain to imputation when he testifies that we die in Adam.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — imputation of Adam's death? unheard-of; then 'sinned in Adam' can stand without sin imputed
english: PLAC. Really—to the imputation of Adam's death? Who ever heard that Adam's death is imputed to us? So my answer—or if you will, my argument—stands: if the proposition "we die in Adam" is true even though Adam's death is not imputed to us, the proposition "we sinned in Adam" can also be true even though Adam's sin is not imputed to us.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — if 'die in Adam' looks to imputation, so does 'sinned in Adam'; only Adam, not Noah etc.
english: GAR. From which I conclude the opposite way from the learned man: if the Apostle's saying "we die in Adam" looks to imputation, then so does what he says about having sinned in Adam. And that saying does look to imputation, as can be shown by a sure reason. For we are not said to die in Noah, nor in any other of our ancestors, but only in Adam. And yet just as we are said to be descended from Adam, so we can be said to be descended from our fathers and all our ancestors.

added_allusions.note: not said to die in Noah

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — discrimination not mere natural propagation, nor Adam-as-origin alone
english: There must be some cause at all of this discrimination. But it is not to be sought simply in the natural conjunction or propagation by which we descend from Adam. For we are no less propagated from our other ancestors, nor less joined to them than to Adam; indeed our communion with them is nearer in time than with Adam. Nor again simply in this, that Adam is the principle of our origin, or the one from whom the human race began. For that can indeed be a legitimate cause why we are said to die in Adam; but it is not a legitimate cause why the same cannot be said of other ancestors. Etc.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — how prove 'die in Adam' means imputation if a non-imputation cause already exists?
english: PLAC. How can it be shown by a sure reason that the Apostle's saying "we die in Adam" looks to imputation, if without imputation there is already a legitimate cause why we are said to die in Adam? For the point was what the Apostle says, not what he does not say. But why is the same not said of other ancestors? If Scripture said and drove home more often that we die in Adam, one might fairly ask why, repeating that matter often, it always remembered one Adam and never other ancestors; now, since it is said only once, it ought not seem strange if other ancestors are passed over in silence, and there is no place to hunt a reason for that silence.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — silence of other ancestors; two reasons: omnes + Adam first source of death
english: Yet if a reason for it must be given, it ought not be fetched from imputation: for at once another question would grow up—why was there not equally in other ancestors, as in Adam, something to be imputed to posterity? And at last one would flee to God's will, which without imputation could be offered here as the reason. But there is no need: other reasons come to hand, and two of them. First, from the word "all." As the Apostle says, we all die in Adam. And it is already plain that all die in Adam alone. Second, it can be drawn from this, that the first source, the first origin of death, is marked. The other ancestors were like channels through which sin and death flowed down from that source into us: Adam alone was the first author of death.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Israel's idolatry called Jeroboam's sin as first author (parallel to Adam)
english: So the common sin of all is called Jeroboam's sin—not Israel's idolatry as of some other king—because Jeroboam had been its first author.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Rom 5: death passed to all because all sinned; omnes same men same way
english: Meanwhile, do you not see that all men are taken in the same way by the Apostle, both when death passes into them and when he says they sinned? Death, he says, passed into all, because all sinned. In both places the word "all" signifies the same men, in the same way.

added_allusions.note: death to all because all sinned

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — otherwise four-term syllogism; conclusion omnes = persons distinct from Adam
english: Otherwise the Apostle's syllogism would be faulty and composed of four terms, which you may form thus: Whoever sinned, into them death passed; all sinned; therefore into all death passed. For in the conclusion the word "all" marks the persons of all men, distinct among themselves and from Adam's person. So in the minor the same word must likewise signify the distinct and separate persons of all men, both among themselves and from Adam.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — distinct persons did not commit Adam's one numerical actual sin (nor one numerical death)
english: But it is already plain that the distinct and separate persons of all men, apart from Adam's person, did not commit that one actual sin, one and the same in number, which Adam committed. And it is as impossible that there should be one numerical actual sin of all the persons of the human race as that there should be one numerical death of all.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR Resp — hard to see how that proves Adam's-sin imputation; no confused hypostasis
english: GAR. Resp. It is hard enough to see and say how the force of this reason assigns the imputation of Adam's sin. For either I am far wrong, or none of those who fight for this imputation ever dreamed that his own person, or any other man's, is confused with Adam's person, or so indistinct as to have coalesced into one hypostasis with him. That cannot even be conceived in the mind. Etc.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — will explain; does not impugn mediate/consequent imputation after corruption
english: PLAC. Since the learned man could not see the force of this reason, I will explain it. Let the reader remember, if he will, that I am not attacking mediate or consequent imputation, which is later than each one's existence and corruption.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — target is immediate/antecedent ('common') imputation as Vir doctus defines it
english: But the immediate and antecedent imputation, which the learned man calls "common" and so describes in Cap. 1 §13: "The common imputation of Adam's sin," he says, "is that by which Adam's sin made not only him guilty, but also implicated the whole race, which was contained in him seminaliter and radicaliter, in the same guilt, already from the time when Adam fell."

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Cap. 2 §17: common/immediate prior to each person's existence and corruption
english: And a little later he says: "But with human nature existing in that principal individual, men can also be said to have existed commonly in him." Existed, that is, distant and separate from Adam's person? I do not think anyone will say that. And Cap. 2 §17: "That common or immediate [imputation]," he says, "just as it was later than Adam's first actual transgression, so it was prior to the personal existence of each man born of Adam, and so also to that corruption which descends into individuals by natural generation, insofar as from the beginning all flowed commonly in Adam."

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — imputation when not yet separate persons; reckoned as one man in Adam
english: That imputation was therefore made when we were not yet persons separate and distant from Adam—or, as the one I was dealing with puts it, when we were considered by God as one man in Adam. Now, I think, you yourself, reader, sufficiently see what force the argument has.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — better rest in Calvin's Clavis: Hebrew 'sin' often quality/condition, not act
english: You would therefore, in my judgment, have done better if, resting in Calvin's interpretation, you had not despised what you could read in the Clavis Scripturae under the name peccatum. He writes that the verb "sinned" in the Qal conjugation often signifies not an action, but an inherent quality, or a man's lot and condition, or to be a sinner, to be guilty—just as Hebrew verbs very often indicate only the existence of a thing, not an action or passion or other motion.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Rom 5 'all sinned in Adam' = became wicked/God's enemies (habitual sense)
english: And a little later: so Rom. 5, in Adam all sinned—that is, they were wicked and enemies of God. Which quasi-habitual sense of the verb and noun "sin" is to be carefully observed.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — Rom 5:12 'in whom all sinned' marks innate evil / all made corrupt through Adam
english: And again, Romans 5: as through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men, in whom all sinned. It signifies not an action but rather a habitual, or innate and essential, evil lot: namely that through Adam all have been made corrupt, etc.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — logicians' definitions mark aptitudo not act (albedo / sight)
english: In the same sense logicians usually note that words set in definitions mark an aptitude, not an act—as when whiteness is defined as a color that scatters sight, that is, that is born apt to scatter sight.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — bad tree / bird analogies: infants and unfledged birds still have the nature
english: So when the Lord says every bad tree bears bad fruit, he would gather poorly who denied that the unregenerate infants of unbelievers are bad trees because they do not yet bear bad fruit. No otherwise than if, reading that every bird flies, he concluded that a chick just hatched, because it does not yet fly, is not a bird.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Sohnius vs Anabaptists: Hebrew peccare actual and habitual (inherent defect)
english: And so to certain Anabaptists objecting—as you do—that "to sin" is an active verb and signifies an action, Georgius Sohnius answered nothing except that among the Hebrews words signify not only actually but also habitually. That is, not only an action, but also an inherent defect and wickedness.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — 'we did not sin actu in original sin except as in Adam' — did we sin actu when he did?
english: For the rest I do not well enough understand those words of yours: "In original sin we did not sin by act, except insofar as we sinned in Adam." What then? Do you mean that we sinned by act in Adam at the time when he sinned?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Zanchius denies actu-sin in Adam: we were not yet actu
english: That Zanchius—whom you praise for your view in chapter 7 of your treatise—denies, adding this reason: because we were not yet in act. For how could it be that, when we were not yet in act, we should sin by act?

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — die actu ⇒ sinned actu; not Adam's act but original vitium inherent in each
english: From which I argue thus: Men die by act. Therefore they have sinned by act. For it is absurd that one who has sinned only in potency, not in act, should be punished in act—and with a most heavy penalty. And yet they did not sin by act in Adam when he sinned actually. There must therefore be another sin because of which men die by act: namely that original vice which is in all and each truly and properly, by act, inherently—as certainly by act as it was in Adam himself.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — 'Adam sinned for all posterity': true as great harm; false as loco nostro
english: Still less do I grasp what you add: when Adam sinned, he sinned for all his posterity. If you mean he sinned to the great harm of all his posterity, nothing is truer. For from that was born the vice that invaded the human race and devoted it to death. But if you mean he sinned in our place, nothing less carefully considered could have been said by you.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Scripture never says loco-sin; Christ truly satisfied / died / suffered in our place
english: For Scripture nowhere says that, and it is exceedingly absurd. Christ did indeed satisfy divine justice in our place—for we were bound to satisfy. All of us had to die; he tasted death in our place. All of us were to be punished; he suffered in the place of all.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — were we bound to sin so Adam would? unheard to sin as another's vadem
english: Were we then bound to sin, so that Adam might sin in our place? For my part it has so far been unheard-of that anyone can sin in another's place as his surety.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — did Adam take our law-keeping part to spare us? Away with such thoughts
english: But perhaps our part was then to keep the law then given to Adam—to hear it, commit it to memory, understand it, carry it out. And Adam, to relieve us of that trouble, put himself in our place to fulfill our duty and play our part. Away with such thoughts.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — if Adam fulfilled the law loco posterorum, posterity would be free in their persons
english: Truly, if Adam had fulfilled that law in the place of all his posterity, his posterity would no longer have been bound to fulfill the same law in their own persons—just as, because Christ satisfied divine justice in our place, we are no longer bound to satisfy it.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — only Adam & Eve then; he did not mean to sin in our place; cannot for non-consenters
english: Certainly, just as at that time there was no human person in the world besides Adam and Eve, so no human person besides those two either could or ought to obey that law for that time. Nor did Adam sin with the mind of sinning in our place; and even if that had been his mind, it is in no one's power to sin in the place of another who does not consent. Nor did nature's law require that he sin in posterity's place, nor did it befit God's goodness and justice to effect and appoint that.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — if Adam sinned loco nostro, why not also punished loco with corruption at once?
english: Besides: if he sinned in our place, and that sin merited the penalty which is sin—namely corruption—tell me, I ask, why was he not also afflicted with that penalty in our place? For at the very moment he sinned, in the same he was made corrupt and vicious and unjust.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — mass-priest analogy: switching persons same moment (sin loco, punish suo)
english: Ought he not to have been punished under the same title under which he sinned, especially at the same moment? Unless you mean that, as a pontifical priest celebrating mass puts on Christ's person and then puts it off, and so plays different persons in almost the same moment, so Adam likewise sometimes represented our person, sometimes sustained his own alone—and in the same moment both sinned in our place and was punished in his own, not ours.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — if punished loco with original-sin penalty, we should not receive the same
english: For if he was chastised in our place with that penalty which is original sin, it does not fit that we should be afflicted with the same penalty: for as he sinned in our place, so he was punished in our place.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Christ parallel: loco punishment frees us; so Adam's loco original would free us too
english: For just as, though we ourselves have sinned in our own persons, yet because Christ was punished in our place we ought not to be punished further: so if for that actual sin Adam was punished in our place by the infliction of original sin, original sin can no longer be inflicted on us for that same sin.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — 'Adam sinned for us' leads to denying our original sin
english: You see where that assertion of yours—that Adam sinned for us—leads you: namely to denying our original sin.

title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC tip — that denial can also be shown by the next argument (imputation vs inherent)
english: Which very thing can also be brought about by this argument, so that you may see more and more how pernicious that opinion is from which I desire and strive to move you.
